This Company is formed for the purpose of raising Brine from the great salt deposits on the estate of A. H. Smith- Barry, Esq., of Marbury, Cheshire, conveying it in iron pipes to the port of Runcorn, on the Mersey, and erecting there ex- tensive works, capable qf ultimately producing 200,000 tons of salt per annum, by which means it can be manufacture,' at a cost considerably less than at existing works in the Salt Dis- tricts, and, also generally for the purposes specified in the Memorandum of Association. The arrangements will include tbe supply of Brine in its natural state to the Chemical Manu- facturers of Puncorn, and a subsequent extension to Widnes and St. Helens Is also contemplated. With these objects in view, the Company acquires the transfer of a very valuable agreement from Mr. Smith-Barry for lease tor a term of 99 years, at royalties under 2d. per ton of salt— the rates ordinarily paid in the districts being about 6d. per ton. Important way-leaves over all the intervening estates, enabling the Brine to be conveyed frotn Northwich to Runcorn, a distance of 13 miles, have also been arranged, and an admi- rable site has been arranged for the Works at the latter town, in close proximity to the Dock and Basin of the Bridgewat, r Navigation, and including •siding communication with the Eond, n and North-Western Railway. By virtue of these leases and way-leaves the Compa .y will possess special, if not absolutely exclusive, advantktes for the supply of Brine to the great consuming centres. The salt trade, with the exception ot coal and Iron, is the most important mineral industry in the kingdom. The Cheshire Salt District yields four-fitths of the total supply, furnishing 1,000,000 tons per annum for export from Liverpool, and upwards of 400,000 to the Chemical Works of Widnes and the neighbouring towns. The existing Salt works in the Cheshire district, though carry- ing on a prosperous trade, are subject to heavy charges in re. spect of due:, freights, !cc., on salt shipped vi the River Weaver to Runcorn and Liverpool, the rates charged to the trade being 2s. ed. and 3s. ed. per ton respectively; the cost of common sat at Northwicb being about Os. per ton. If destined for export from Runcorn, salt under the present system requi es tranship- ment from the barges into seagoing vessels. These heavy charges will be avoided, and this Company will be in a r ositi n to command the bulk of the coasting and foreign trade from Runcorn, averaging at present 200,000 tons per annum, and also largely supply the Liv.npool market. Coal or slack, which is largely consumed in the manufat tare of salt, is cheaper sit Runcorn than at Northwich.

By 'acquiring the various concessions above detailed, this Company will effect a saving equivalent to 20 per cent, on all salt manufactured at the Runcorn works ; and this in addition to the saving in the cost of coal; while the exceptionally favour- able rates on which the royalties are based will enable the Brine to be delivered at Runcorn at lower charges than are generally paid by the salt manufacturers at Northwich. After the most careful calculations including thecost of wear and tear, &c., it is anticipatea that: the profit on the manu- facture of salt alone at Runcorn will enable the Company to pay dividends of at least 120 per cent, on the capital subscribed. A further source of eventual profit is anticipated from the supply of Brine in- its natural state to the chemical manufac- turers of Widnes, St. Helens, and Runcorn, for utilisation in various branches of their trade. If satisfactory arrangements can be made with the authorities and manufacturers, the Direetors will be willing, to supply Widnes with Brine by means of lighters, as soon as possible after the completion of the line of pipes from Northwich to Runcorn. The salt works in the Northwieh district, in consequence of the continual extraction of Brine, are subject to such occasional subsidences as occurred in December last when six works were disabled. The works of the Company at Runcorn will not be subject to such conthigency ; they will be built upon solid ground nearly 13 miles distant from the Salt Districts. Particular attention is called to the annexed report of J. F. Bateman, Esq., C.E.,F.R.5., the Company's Engineer, in which the works for raising the Brine and convey- ing it to Runcorn are described as of a very simple character. Mr. Bateman estimates their cost, exclusive of that of the Evaporating Works, at £106.000, Contracts have been entered into with Messrs. Smith, Finlayson, and Co., of Westminster, for the execution of the general works, and with Messrs. James Watt and Co., of Soho, Birmingham, for the machinery, at prices within the above estimate. The various agreements for leases and way-leaves have been granted to Mr. Thomas Coglan Horsfall, but only as agent for Mr. Godfrey Joachim Aman, who is the promoter of the Com- Pany, and who joins Mr. Horsfall in the assignment of these agreements. The price agreed to he paid be Mr. Amen for the transfer of these very valuable agreements Is the sum of £27,500 in cash, to- gether with 1,250 fully paid-up shares in the Company of au) each. Mr Amen will pay a sum of £lO,OOO to the trustees, in order to provide 'lite, est at the rate of 5 per cent. per aanum on the paid-up capital of the Company during the period of construction up to the delivery of the Brine at Runeorn. Ile also bears and will indemnify the Company against all ex- I penscs incidental to its formation. with the exception of the charges of its own solicitors, and a sum equivalent to If per cent. on the amount of the present issue to pay for brokerage, &c. Application will be made to the London Stock Excluusge for SO official quotation of the shares of the Company. The Contracts which have been entered into are the follow- ing, and may be seen at the offices of the Solicitors to the Com- pany, Me‘ifirs. Baxtrers, and Co., 5 and 6, Victoria-street, Westminster. SCIENTIFIC NOTES. Another chamber with the mystical cow and the descrip- tion of the destruction of mankind has been discovered at Thebes. A tomb recently discovered has furnished some amulets, but 12 mummy cases found in it are said to have been broken up. It is then sifted to get rid of the dust, and the powder is treated with gelatine, and shaped into any form required.—Design and Work. PLANTS BLOOMING WITHOUT EAUTH. —M. Alfred Dumesnil, a son-in-law of Jules Mithelet, and the editor of the first edition of Edgar Quinet's Works, claims to have made an useful and interesting discovery—how to preserve plants in a perfectly vigorous state without any earth. Since November, 1880, the date at which his researches proved successful, he has, with the exception of a six weeks' stay in Paris, been constantly taking plants from the ground and applying his process to them; has never found the least interruption in their vegetative functirens; on the con- trary, winter and spring plants have blossomed with a vigour which, as an experienced horticulturist, he has never seen in his garden.. With the shelter of a glass, helebores taken up at the end of November and the middle of December have remained from two and a half to three months in blossom. Other plants, primroses, daisies, violets, auriculas, dtca have not only been in bloom for three months, but have thrown out new bads. Bulbous roots, small .shrubs, exotic plantit; such as azaleas and cyclamens,•take equally Well to the pro- cess. M. Dtunesnil exhibited some specimens of plants blooming Witheut earth in the Square Solverino, in Rouen, last December; and at his home in Vaseceuil, about 14 miles from that city, anyone may have ocular demonstration of the results he has obtained. In any light, the diecovery is an interesting and an important one, as its applications are numberless, and the fresh scope it would give to the floral decoration of interiors is delightful to contemplate. CHINESE NEWSFAFERS.—UntiI a few decades ago adver- tisements were unknown in Chinese journalism. Such ansoancements were only to be found at the street corners. Here and there loose leaflets were distributeil, containing little else than a sensational story of robbery, as the break- ing of an armed band into a pawnshop, or an *neon* of the death of a man-eating tiger. From an article in the Austrian Menatschift for the East, by Herr F. Hirth, of Shanghai, 'we 'learn that of existing newspapers only one is due to patch y Chineee initiative, the so-called King-pan, or Pekin Gazette, which, solely confined to official decrees, can scarcely be compared with Eurpean journals. The, King-pao is the organ of the Government, and disdains to concern itself with non-official matters or anything connected with trade. Advertisements are not to be thought of. On the other hand, it may be regarded as a happy sign of the times that the idea of newspapers in the European. sense, or first started by Europeans, is becoming more and more understood and acted on in the coast provinces. There exist at present several papers printed in Chinese characters, partly in Hongkong, partly in Shanghai. Amoy has also had for some little time it Chinese organ. The Shen-pao, a daily paper, founded by .Mr. Ernest. Major, winch, under eminent editorship, advocates the progressive interests of the European party, numbers its Chinese subscribers by the ten thousand, and is read not only in Shanghai and the neighbourhood, but also here and there in the-Interior of China, especially in the provincial chief towns and in the Treaty Ports. is an opposition organ, was founded several years ago by the anti-European or Mandarin party, the Sin-pao, edited after the model of the other, but conducted on a different platform. The Sic-pan has also a large con- tingent of readers. Both papers contain a full reprint of the King -pao ; the Chinese reader thus saves his subscription to the official organ, and receives besides a large supply of news, which, after he gets used to this kind of reading, in- terests him exceedingly. A stroll through the Chinese , quarter of Shanghai yields the best evidence of this. At almost every door will be found people diligently studying one or other of the two papers. If we examine the contents of these sheets we find first of all, after the reprint of the State Gazette, a leading article. In this is seen the chief differvee between the two party papers, unless the subject is purely literary, when there is no oppartunity for airing political prejudices. To the latter belong, indeed, questions which with us have long ceased to have anything to do with politics. After this follow matters which, for European readers are not only tedious, but difficult to understand, mixed news, partly translated from English papers, partly collected by special reporters from among the people. These news contain mostly matters of fact, and are as trustworthy as in most of the European papers. A considerable rile is Played by the accounts of the sittings of the Mixed Courts. Then come copies of proclamations by the local mandarins, and lastly advertisements, among which will be found announcements of special European firms. WHAT IS LOVE? Is Love a pretty fairy bright. With silvery wings, ano robed in white? Is it a nymph, or little sprite. That gambols la the pale moonlight? Is it a sylph, surpassing fah' Which roams at will thrungh realms of air' Is it a s ene in fairy land; A chorus from the white-robed band? Is it a bird of Paradise, • Which by its beauty cloth melee ? Is it a star, whose dazzling light Doth sheer the gloom of darkest night? Is it an angel robed in white, Fr, m heavenly plata in realms of light? ; Love's a feeling, holy, pure, Which makes us all life's thorns endure; That uproots vile and sinful weeds, And prompts us on to nobler deeds Rich blessings follow in its train. And makes us from bac, deeds refrain. It makes the mourner's tears to cease, And breathes a calm and holy peitce. Its worth is more than untold gold, Fresh beauties from it e'er unfold. 'Tis an attribute of God Blost High. And originated is the sky; 'Tis the nature of the spirits there, The bright, the holy angels fair. St. Helens. J. G. PIOSERSGILL.

Do not be ashamed of hard work. Work, but work for hall- oe rather than be idle. Be your own master, and do not let society or .fashion swallow you up individually—hat, coat, and boots. Do not eat up or wear out all you can s earn. Compel your selfish body to spare something for profits saved. Be stingy te your own appetite, but merci- tut 'for others' necessities. Help others, and ask not for yourselves. See that you are proud, too. Let your pride be of the right kind. George looked 'astonished, but answered the pleasaet-faced, tired-looking _gentleman with a " Yes, I'm tolerably rich." A pause oc- curred, and then another question, "Flow rich are you?" ' A PRIVATE STILL.—A revenue officer was sent into an illicit whisky-distilling district in Kentucky. He knew illicit distilling was going on, but he could get no balls to work upon. Coming to an Irishman, who was terribly drunk, the officer tapped him on the shoulder, and' said, "My man, do you want to make ten dollars ?" "Is it ten dollars?" said Pat; "sure and I do." "Then," said the s officer, "show me a private still." "I'll do that same; fol- low me, yer honour.' The officer followed across lots of fields to the camp of a company of soldiers which had been sent there to aid the revenue officers. The soldiers were in line—dress parade. "Do you see that red-headed man ?" asked Pat, pointing to one of the soldiers. "Yes," replied 'the officer. "He is," said Pat," my brother. He's been in the service twelve years. He'll be a corporal after a while, but he is a ` private still.'" Count Janbert was wonderfully happy at repartee, and in his sallies was utterly indifferent as to whether it was a friend or an enemy who suffered. If, however, he happened to compromise himself, he had a happy knack of setting „himself right in a moment. On one occasion having been highly pleased with Marshal Soult, be made the illustrious soldier the butt of innumerable epigrams. The Marshal, 'hearing of this, at one of Louis Philippe's receptions turned his back upon the Count just as he was stepping forward to Salute him, some thirty gentlemen being present. "Mon- sieur le Marsh," said Count Jaubert, with the utmost song fraid," I have been told you do not look upon me as one of your friends; I'm delighted to find there is no ground Jpr the rumour." "How so, monsieur?" "Because," replied the Count, "you are not in the habit of turning your back to the enemy." The Marshal, it is perhaps need- less to say, at once held out his hand to Count Jaubert. AN AGED TREE.—" Old Moses," one of the mightiest sylvan patriarchs of California, was mercilessly cut down a few weeks age, and the greater portion of his venerable re- mains have already been sold to the timber merchants of San Francisco. This colossal tree, judging by the number of rings contained in a sound section of its trunk, had at- tained the amazing age of four thousand eight hundred and forty-one years when the fell fiat was issued for its de- struction. The hollow portion of its huge and massive stem afforded standing room for nearly three hundred full- grown men. Its term of existence was a longer one than that of the world's known, or at least authenticated, his- tory; and it must have been a "brave green tree" when Noah built his Ark. That so extraordinary a relic of the dim prehistoric past should have been thus ruthlessly made away with—unless its sacrifice were the outcome of some imperative necessity—cannot but be a source of universal regret; and we can readily imagine what the feelings of Professor Wendell Holmes, the true lover and chivalric champion of giant trees, must have been when the dread tidings reached his ear that" Old Moses" had fallen before the axe. CARLYLE'S FAVOURITE HO.—What he loves to delineate is the man who can discern and grope his way honestly by a little light struggling through a world of darkness—the man whose gloom is deep, but whose lucidity of vision, so far as it go, is keen—the man who is half hypochondriac, half dev aee, but wholly indomitahle, like Mehemet, Crom- wa, Johnson. Every hero he had was great in proportion as he displayed at once this profound impression of the darkness and difficulty of life, and this vehement dictatorial mode of acting on the glimpses or visions he had by way of showing valour in defiance of the darkness. Carlyle's charac- teristic delight in Odin and the Scandinavian mythology is a mere reflection of this strong appreciation of the religion of the volcano, the thunder-cloud, and the lightning-flash, mingled with a certain grim enjoyment of the spectacle of the inadequacy of human struggle. If Carlyle loved also tv describe keen, clear wits like Jeffrey and Voltaire--a he revelled, too, in the picture of thin, acrid natures like Robespierre's, it was as foils to his favourite portraits of grim, vehement, dictatorial earnestness.—Good Words for ftpril. CHOOSING TIM WOOD FOR THE OLD VIOLINS.—Betore a beam was bought, the master passed his hand over the surface. He could tell by touch the density of its fibre. Then he would take two equal slips of deal and weigh them, and judge of their porossness. The very appearance of the wood would guide him to its probable vibrational powers. Then he would, perchance before leaving the market, cat strips of equal length, and elicit their relative intensities by striking their tongues. He would often select for a definite purpose, looking for a soft, porous piece, or a specially hard and close-fibred grain—a certain appearance he would in- stinctively associate with rare acoustic properties. The seller would be eager to find the pieces, useless to other customers, priceless to an Andreas Amati, for he was sure that the viol maker would bay whaf suited him at a long price. After the lapse of nearly two centuries, we can trace such favourite beams by peculiar stains, freckles, and grain- ngs. When;after cutting up a dozen trees, once in two or hree years a piece of fine acoustic wood was found, it was kept for the master's best work. The same pine beam will crop up in the bellies of Stradianarius at an interval of •years. -Another can be traced in the violins of Joseph Gnarnerins, and after his death Carlo Bergonzi got hold of the remnants of it, and we detect it by a certain stain in the fibre. The anxiety to retain every particle of a preeious 'piece of wood is seen in the subtle and delicate patching and repatching of backs and bellies. The seams are only dis- coverable by a microscope, so perfect is the cabinet work. Fausr Lerrisne—The Estates Gazette gives an instance of the low terms on which land may now be obtained, the particulars of which were supplied by a farmer., A farm of 250 acres were offered te him for a year rent free, and he took it. It is rather thin-skinned heavy land, but it has all been drained, and new farm buildings have been erected on it recently. Until four years ago, too, it was well farmed; but there is some land adjoining it out of cultivation, and covered with docks, thistles, and other weeds, and it is sup- posed that the owner feared his land might get into a similar state if not cultivated. After this farm had been taken, the owner of a small farm of about 50 acres near by came to the tenant, and asked him if he would take it. The tenanteaid he would, ender certain conditions. "What will you give me for it ?" was the next question. "Nothing at all," was the reply. "Then what offer do you make?" "I will farm it for a year, without paying any rent, if you will pay half the cost of the labour," said the tenant. In the end the tenant agreed to take the farm. For the first two years he is to pay no rent, and then for six years longer he is to pay 15s. per acre. On both these farms, which are let, one till Michaelmas, 1881, and the other till Michael- mas, 1882, rent free, there is a tithe of 7s. per acre. PREPARING FERMENTING MATERIALS FOR HOT BEDS, Stc.—TO so many uses can &heap of fermenting materials upon which a frame is fixed be applied that a hint as to pre- paration may be useful.' Fermenting materials should con- sist of sweet stable manure and tree leaves only, anti it undergoes the process of sweetening by allowing as little decompoiition as possible. To prevent this some little care is necessary. Good stable litter requires to be turned— shaking it well up at each operation—three times only; barrowing it where necessary, and making the bed up at last being counted as a fourth turning. In turning a heap over the second time, do not, as is customary, begin at one side, and continue straight through, taking all as it comes; but first of all, take the whole outer layer of the heap off to a foot in depth, and lay it down as a bed for the remainder. When any part has become too dry, moisten it with clean water carefully distributed with a rosed watering-can. It Is not always advisable to put all the shorter droppings with the same, as these too readily hasten the decay of the whole. Where a mixture is made, half leaves and half stable litter, it is not judicious to mix up the leaves with the litter until the bed is being made up; the sweating which the leaves undergo in a heap by themselves amply prepares them, without further neutralising their best properties by admix- ture with the litter. By no means permit the litter from kennels, ferret hutches, or the like, to be mixed up with the above, for if you do, it will Inas your best efforts. What is required is an uniformly heating mass, not wet nor too. dry, but if masses of foreign matter exist within the heap, It gives rise to a most injurious steam, which very fre- quently is known to destroy whole frames filled with tender plants. SUCCESSFUL POULTRY KEEPING.—In 1878, nearly 783 millions of eggs were imported into the country, of the ag- gregate value of £2,512,000. Each year the consumption continues to increase, as people become aware of the fact eggs are a most nourishing and excellent food, suitable alike for•the strong or thedelicate. Here, then, is a very large sum of money, which is being paid annually to other coun- tries for an article which might easily and cheaply be pro- duced at home, The first thing to consider in poultry- keeping is what accommodation there is for the birds. I Can they have their freedom to roam over the fields, or by the roadside, or in the farmyard? For any one of these are the most favourable conditions for poultry-keeping, and with their liberty, as the weather becomes milder, the birds Will, in most cases, be able to find for themselves the greater por- tion of their food in the shape of insects, grubs, dm ; but If they are confined in a run all the year round, depeidlng entirely upon their owner for every grain of corn consumed, there is little to be surprised at if birds kept under such condition do not prove very remunerative. If the rearing of poultry and the sale of eggs can be made a profitable undertaking in other countries, whf, should it not be so here? It is true our climate is more variable; still the hens lay just as many eggs here as they do abroad, that is, if the right sort are kept, and the old and worthless specimens are eipher sold or killed. With cattle, whether :kept for dairy purposes or for the market, no practical man who ex- pects to obtain a balance on the right side would ever think' of retaining year after year a number of old and worn out animals, which consume just as mach food as the younger and more profitable animals. Neither could he dream of allowing the same to breed i,n and in for generations with- out any Cross to improve and give fresh vigour and strength of constitution to his. herd. And yet this Is what is often allowed to go on in the poultry yard, and still people com- plain that their fowls do not lay, that many die during the winte;t and they are most unprofitable things to keep. All this might easily be altered and a very different aspect given to poultry-keeping if people would only sell or kill off their se eedy, small, and closely-bred-in birds so fre- quently seen around farmhouses. What is required is a good, useful, cross-bred bird, either between the Dorking and game, or Dorking and Brahma, or game and Brahma. These are the birds which, when they have reached maturity, are capital layers, large in body, and with good cuts of meat on the breast. And until such birds as these are kept and the old ones got rid of each year—keeping , none beyond their second season—so long will poulty be found untemnnerative. PARSNIPS.—This is a crop of greater value than is gener- ally appreciated, otherwise parsnip beds would be as com- mon as onion beds, which is certainly not the case in all dis- tricts. There is no root so serviceable as a substitute for potatoes daring a Simon of scarcity as this, while it is even more nutriti9us than potatoes are, and when once a taste for it has been acpuife4lts flavour, is agreeable to most palat i. A deeply-workedpoil is ,essential for parthips, and manure should not be dug in immediately before sowing. The drills should be 15 inches apart, the seed being sown thinly and covered half an inch deep. It must be new, as old seed will not germinate, and the sooner it is in the ground the better. ABIERICAN RAILWAY CHARGES ON ENGLISH SALT.—A memorial to the New York State Legislature, reported in the American Dairyman, indicates a grievance felt by , American farmers similar to that which is being experienced , in this country. Similar in character,but different in kind; or whereas here we complain that :the railways favour foreign goods to the injury of home producers; there the complaint is that foreign goods are taxed in a one-sided way , by railways as well as by the State,th the heavy loss of thei consumer. The rate of carriage on 290 ton of foreign salt I from Albany to Buffalo is 216 do!.; for the same quality of domestic salt it is only 82.8 dol. And it appears that the use of American salt is a detriment to the dairy interest of the State—all the let prizes at the two great International Dairy Shows, New York, having been taken by butter and cheese salted with English salt. Tax IMPORTANCE OF SOWING GOOD SEED has always been coneidered one of the primary rules of agriculture. Yet how often is it neglected, or at least not implicitly ad- hered to? Some who think they faithfully carry the in- junction into practice do nothing of the kind,simply because they only care to sow sound germs of a low order, whereas they might just as well sow a superior variety, which would he calculated to yield produce of a far higher quality. Our leading seedsmen devote themselves to an extremely benefi- cial work when they select the best from the best in any plant produce, to procure pedigree varieties, and experienced farmers are well aware how much better it is to sow some ef the choicer varieties of turnips and mangel wurzel which I have thus been selected and cultivated rather than the com- moner kinds. But the same rule extends to the cereals, and "other grain. Mr. Hallett, of Brighton, was the first to awaken attention to the importance of employing critical selection, so as to obtain pedigree varieties of corn; and now all our leading seed houses advertise choice varieties, which have been cultivated, and are calculated to produce larger and better crops if employed in the right way. In sowing barley, the variety selected may not only affect the return in produce, but go a long way in determining whether the crop will be a first-class one in quality for malting purposes. Also as regards oats, a plump, fine seed sample wilt usually produce fruit of the same character but pithless, long-tailed seeds, are apt to yield crops of the; like valueless ilk. For potatoes the importance of good seed is all the more important from pones few kinds being absolutely disease proof, while certain others are much less liable to be injured than the commoner sorts, although they may not, perhaps, be deemed absolutely free from affection. No one in his senses would surely think of planting largely with the varieties which are most susceptible to disease in- fluencee if a more healthy kind were available. We shall always probably be compelled to depend on horticulturists for bringing into existence new sorts, which at first are im- pregnable against atmospheric affection; but in all proba- bility one and all, after being planted several years in suc- cession from mattings,become less robust and at last succumb to the disease. For successful potato culture, a rule which should be faithfully observed is to plant from large sets , instead of small ones. There must be some cause which' prevented the latterifrom arriving at full development and made the others fine, and those who study the laws of natnrr Must perceive that "like produces like." Neither shoal more than one eye, or at the most two eyes, be left in th set. It is much better to raise a few stout stalks than number of puny ones.—Farmers' Chronicle. TRUE SAYINGB.-A jest driven too far brings home hate. -A headstrong man and a fool may wear the same cap.- A great man's foolish sayings pass for wise ones.-A hand- saw is a good thing, but not to shave with.-A joke never gains an enemy, but often loses a friend.-A joyful evening may follow a sorrowful morning.-A handful of common- sense is worth a bushel of learning.-A great man will not trample on a worm, nor speak to an emperor. • DAMAGES.-" I am a peaceable man," said the intruder, grasping his club with both his hands, "but if you don't come down with seventeen dollars fifty cents damages for my lacerated feelings, the bombardment will begin at once." The owner of the dog also said that he was sorry that the dog had bitten the intruder's son. "Why, he ain't my son," said the intruder. "Whose son is. be then?" asked the astonished owner of the dog. "He is the son, of a friend of mine who owed me seventeen dollars fifty cents; but he is poor, and the only available assets he had was these dog-bites on his body, which he turned over to me for col- lection." "Well, I'll be shot!" "Oh, you needn't com- plain; you are getting off dog-cheap! I ought to make you pay in advance for the next time that boy is going to be bit.m-Galvestou Paper. An exceptionally large number of garottting cases have recently occured at Bradford. , It is stated that Mr. Ross has consented to contest St. Ives in the Conservative interest.
Two boys were sent to prison for seven days by the Wandsworth magistrate for setting fire to the furze on Wim- bledon Common.
- THE CENSUS OF 1881.

On Tuesday fourteen or fifteen men were injured, eight of them seriously, through the breakdown of a crane at the Tyne Engine Works Ousebourne. It is stated on authority that Mr. Edward 'E. Kay, Q.C., has been offered and has accepted the judgeship vacant by the resignation of Vice-Chancellor Malins. A woman named Jeanes, the wife of a ,labourer living at Pulham, has committed suicide by hanging, from the effects of a religious mania. Some rioting occurred at Basingstoke on Sunday in con- nection with the S dvation Army proceedings. The Mayor read the Riot Act, and the military speedily cleared the streets. A coroner's jury, at Sudbury, have returned a verdict of wilful murder against Suatanah Bowers, wife of a labourer, who, on Saturday, cut the threats of her two children, despite the efforts of an elder girl, aged twelve, to pre- vent her. The unfortunate woman afterwards cut her own throat.

On Monday a meeting of Manchester merchants inte- rested in foreign trade, and particularly in that with the East, unanimously adopted a memorial to Lord Hartington in favour of representatives of the Imperial and Indian Governments being deputed to take part in the forthcoming International Monetary Conference at Paris. At the Carmarthen Nice Court, a youth named NPCann, charged with fraudutent enlistment, was remanded because the' magisterial text-book regarding offences was not in court, and the d puty justices' clerk could not advise the Bench how to act. After some hours delay the prisoner was again brought 'up and fined £l. Sir William Knollys has written to the Committee of the National Eisteddfod of Wales stating that the Prince of Wales cannot comply with their wish that His Royal High- ness should be a president of the institution. The Controller of • the Household of the Duke of Edinburgh, to whom a similar request was addressed, has made a like I reply. At the half-yearly meeting of the Caledonian Railway Company, the Chairman said they had been exposed to the severest competition, which had impoverished all engaged in it. They had, however, carr,ied more passangers, mer- chandise, and minerals, and earned more revenue than in any corresponding half year. A dividend of 24 per cent was declared. The Chancellor of the Exchequer has informed the To- bacco Trade Association that he is absolutely precluded from entertaining at present any proposal for repealing the extra tobacco clutz imposed by the late Government. The right bon. gentleman points out that the immediate loss to the revenue would be such as he has no means of meeting in the present state of our revenue and expenditure. A serious riot occurred at Reading on Sunday afternoon in connection with the Salvation Army, which has com- menced holding its services in a large boathouse. The morning service was broken up, and in the afternoon the mob attacked the two leaders, and ill-treated them in a brutal manner. Thty were compelled to seek shelter in a neighbouring house, which the mob.sarrounded for several hours.

At Sheffield, on Saturday night, James Hall, a cutler, murdered his wife by battering in her head with a hatchet. He also attempted to murder his daughter. Hall is said to have been leading a dassipated life and to have been living on his wife's earni,ll,s, and frequent quarrels had been the result. The murdered woman is described as having been extremely industrious. The murderer made a full confes- sion of his geilt. The official liquidators of the West of England Bank have issued a statement showing that the whole of the three mil- lions and a quarter of liabilities, save about £54,000, have been paid, and the assets to meet this are estimated at £78,001. This shows a surplus for return to the share- holders, but ens of the largest of the items forming the Rssets may possibly be the subject of a Chancery suit and heavy, loss. The Registrar-General's returns just presented to the Lord- Lieutenant of Ireland show that the number of emigrants who left Irish ports in 1880 was 95,857—An increase of 45,493 as compared with 1879—the numbeeof males being 50,189 ; females, 48,088. From the Ist of May, 1851, to the 31st December' 1880, the total emigration 'from Ireland has been 2,837,187. An inquest was held at Sheffield, an Tuesday, on she body of Mary Ann Hall. A verdict of wilful Murder was teturned agaiust her husband, and the prisoner on being taken back to the police offices had a num* escape of being lynched. For some hours a great crowd of people had gathered near the hotel where the inquest was held, and when Hall. ssas brought out, handcuffed, he had to be protected from the moblay six policemen. The people tried repeatedly to drag him away from the police, and yelled, hooted, and called him "Coward, coward." A man in comparatively humble life in Retford, who had reeided quite happily with his wife, took in a young man as a lodger, and he seems to have impressed himself favourably upon the mind of his landlady. On her husband returning home from his work, one day last, week,,he found that his "better half" had disappeared, taking a box containing her wearing apparel with her. There are no children to suffer from the neglect of a mother, and the only injured person is the husband himself. He has inquired the whereabouts of his wife, and finding out her deetination, he has resigned himself to the loss he has sustained. . The authorities have at last got over the Fenian scare, and ammunition ie now being issued for the purpose of com- mencing class-firing on the different rifle-ranges. We have always held that, the precautions taken by the Government were perfectly unnecessary, and calculated to bring about the, very evil which they were intended to prevent. There can be no doubt that the hurried orders of our terrified superiors produced a very uneasy feeling for a time but events have proved how entirely superfluous these orders were, and the Volunteer Force for a time felt itself, to speak the truth; placed in a somewhat difficult position.—Volunteer Review. 'At a great Conservative demonstration, in Glasgow, on Monday, Mr. Ashrnead-Bartlett, M.P., said the party who I involved England in unnecessary, expensive, and dis- honourable wars were the peace-at-any-price party. The English people were not the poor-spirited wretches the men of Birmingham imagined, and the Government that sacri- ficed their rights would learn to rue it ere many menthe. With reference to the Traasvaal war, he argued that Mr. Gladstone's Midlothian speeches were the incentives to rebellion. The Government stirred up the country , by their unfortunate harangues, conducted the war with dis- credit, and had concluded it with dishonour. The annual meeting of the Hertfordshire Liberal Regis- tration Association was held in London, on Monday, Mr. R. Pryor presiding. After reading the annual report, the pre- sident, in the name of the association, presented Mr. Stephen Austin, of the Hertfordshire Mercury, with a gold watch land the balance of £3OO, subscribed in recognition of fifty year' services gratuitously rendered to the Liberal cause in Hertfordshire. Mr. Austin having replied, and reviewed the progress of Liberalism in Hertfordshire since 1827, a resblution was passed expressing cordial approval of the course pursued by the Government in hems and foreign affairs. An alarming fire, which resulted in loss of life and great destruction of property, took place on Tuesday morning in Manchester. About half-pastlwelve a policeman discovered that the warehouse of Messrs. John Haslam and Co., cotton spinners and ivanufacturers, was on fire. Owing to the position of the warehouse, which .is situated in a narrow portion of the town, it was difficult to get at the horsing rooms. The warehouse, which is seven storeys high, was gutted, and a very valuable stock of muslins and fancy goods was totally destroyed. The damage is estimated at r cope or £BO,OOO. During the progress of the fire a sad accident occurred to three fireman who were playing on the flames at the bottom of the Staircase. A bundle of blazing checks fell upon them and completely encircled them. When they were rescued one, John Earley, was found to be dead, and two others, Engineer Stevenson and Fireman Griffiths, so badly injured that their recovery is doubtful. In the Arches Court, on Saturday, an application was made for a fresh order of commitment against the Rev. R. W. Enraght, the well-known—by ream of the proceedings against him—vicar of Bordesley, near Birmigham. It was proved that the rev, gentleman immediately after his release on a curious technicality by the Court of Appeal had resorted to his former practices, and had repeatedly offended against the monition under whicl, he still labours. Lord Penzance declin d, however, to grant the application for a fresh writ of significavit, on the ground that Mr. Enraght by his appeal to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal—which was against him on some points— would open up the whole question of the constitution and power of the Court of Arches to deal with offences under the Public Worship Regulation Act. If, said Lord Penzance, the House of Lords were to decide that the proceedings had been valid throughout, "it was to be expected that Mr. Enraght's doubts would at last be set at rest, and that, as a clergyman of the Eetablished Church and a good subject of the Queen," he would undertake in future to obey the decree of the Court, and not compel it to send him to prison again. His Lordship intimated that he should expect Mr. Enraght's appeal to be prosecuted with all reasonable speed. The action for libel brought by Mr. Lawson, proprietor of the Daily Telegraph, against Mr. Labouchere, M.P., had a not altogether unexpected ending on Monday. The jury, after a prolonged consultation, represented that they were unable to agree, and they were therefore dischuged, it being intimated that they were about equally divided in opinion. Whether the case lie to be re-tried must depend, as the Lord Chief Justice remarked, upon the good sense of the parties. In the course oran elaborate summing-up, Lord Coleridge said it was impossible not to hold that some of the Tele- graph's articles on Lord Beaconsfield went beyond the line of fair and legitimate public criticism. For a jourr_al to sneer at Mr. Disraeli because of his Jewish faith was beyond the line of such comment, especially when it was remem- bered that the proprietors of the journal belonged them= selves to the Hebrew persuasion. Referring to Mr. Las-eon's contention that a newspaper editor was not a proper subject. for public criticism, his lordship said he could not altogether, accept it. Here, he observed, was a pap r with a circule.s tion of 220,000 copies, mit and appealing to a million read, and he could not agree that it was not legitimate to inquire' whether the person who was wielding this great instrumenk —isha.was at the other end of this machine—was a giant, or a
" Relish for tea—Hartley's New Marmalade, 21b.

The census of England and Wales will be taken on the 4th of next month. The work is appropriately termed by the Registrar-General a great national undertaking, and the arrangements for its accurate completion are well advanced by the officials to whom the duty is entrusted. The Act of Parliament providing for the taking of this decennial census was passed last Session, and by it the superintendence of the work is wholly vested in the Local Government Board. Acting on behalf of that body„ the Registrar-General, Sir B. P. Henniker, is the executivi officer, and to him the super- intendent registrars and registiars of sub-districts are re- sponsible for the performance of the work. The Act pro- vides for the formation of the registration districts into enumerators' divisions, for the appointment of the enumera- tors, and for all the details of the work. The Registrar- General, again, has issued an elaborate book of instructions for the guidance of registrars and enumerators, for the issu- ing and collection of the schedules—in fact, the directions given are of the minutest and amplest character, and calcu- lated, in the hands of intelligent and capable men, to ensure the absolute accuracy of the enumeration of the millions of the population. The registrars have already snapped out and made plans of their respective districts, and forwarded them, with the list of enumerators, to the Census Office, where they will be revised and finally settled prior to the delivery of the schedules to the qccupiers a dwellings, which will commence on the 28th inst. On or before Satur- day, the 2nd April, the enumerators must have completed the delivery of all schedules, the full term of six daysbeing considered ample for each enumerator to cover the area en- trusted to him. Monday, April 4th, is the Census Day, when all the schedules must be collected. They will be filled up at each dwelling or place where they are left with the dames of every soul living thereat ift midnight on Sun- day, April 3rd. The forms are of the same nature as those used in 1871. The information sought to be recorded is the name, sex, age, occupation, and residence of each individual of the population. Nothing else is required to be entered in the schedules, and in some districts the registrars are taking what seems to be a desirable precaution of issuing notices explaining to the inhabitants that po religious census or enumeration for School Board purposes will be attempted, and is not allowed. In the formation of districts it is assumed that an efficient enumerator will be able to visit 200 houses in a town in one day, but no district is to be so 'large as not to admit of all the houses in it being visited without difficulty in the course of a single day by the enu- merator. Forkpublic institutions having more than 200 in- mates, the master or head of each is to be appointed the endmerator, with a scale of allowances accordingly. The Customs officers are instructed to enlimerate persons on board ships, fishing smacks, and vessels of all kinds, except those belonging to the Royal Navy (which will be enumer- ated by the Admiralty), in the ports, harbours, and docks of England and Wales. The enumeration of persons in boats, barges, .bc., on canals, rivers, and other inland waters not within the 'limits of any port within the jurisdiction of the Customs, must be provided for by making such canals and navigable waters well-defaaed parts of the enumeration districts. Schedules for vessels are specially provided. The enumerators are provided with books wherein to record all schedules delivered and collected. They will have to deliver to the registrars all their schedules, books. and other docu- ments pertaining to the census before Monday, the I,lth April. The superintendent registrars must perfortn the im- portant duty of revising, checking, and eartitying to the correctnesS of the enumerators' books. All househoklers' schedules most be forwarded by the registrars to the Census Office before Monday, April 25th,,and tlten the analysis and collation of the census will be commenced at headquarters, and probably by midsummer an abstract will be ready. With respect to the census about to, be undertaken it may be interesting to state that so long ago as 1751, when the facilities for the work were not comparable with those now at command a most painstaking effort was made by the Go- vernment to ascertain the population of riareat .Britain, and thee estimate finally enabled was 7,392,000. This is con- sidered to hate been a very fair approximation;* A contro- versy arose towards the end of last century as to the popu- lation of Great Britaiii, some maintaining that through war, famine, and other causes, we were numerically decreasing. A general and' considerable interest was excited in the ques- tion, and the result was the first census that was taken in this country. It was bbtained during the administratioa of Mr. Pitt in the year 1801. 'The work was carefully under- taken, and when the returns , had been compiled the result showed that the entire, population of Great Britain was 10,834,623, which, added to the estimated population of Ireland, made a grand total of 16,095,000. Since then a census has been taken every ten years. The attempt to take the statistics of Ireland in 1811 is stated to have been some- what unsuccessful, and the accuracy of the enumeration the decade following was doubtful. The returns of the popula- tion of our Sister Isle in the year 1831 were more reliable, but were corrected three years after in order that it might form the basis of a new system of education.. Subsequent , returns have been trustworthy, and have furnished besides ' important statistics regarding the agricultural condition of the country. The returns for England and Wales have been, it is believed, remarkably aCcurate. As the population in 1801 was estimated at 16,095,000, we find that at the end of sixty years more than 13i millions had been added to the resident inhabitants of the country, the total population in 1861 standing at 29,334,788. On the 3rd of April, 1871, the date on which the last census was taken, the population of the United Kingdom was 31,817,108, consisting of 15,549,271 males and 16,267,838 females. The area of the errantry is 77,513,585 acres. Between 1801 and 1871 the population of the kingdom had increased by 15,722,108, the increase from 1861 having been 2,482,320. Many interesting facts have been gathered in the course of these periodical enume- rations of the population. In 1801 there were only 101 per- sons in Birkenhead, but after the lapse of but sixty years, so rapid had been the development of this town, that its resident population numbered 51,649, and ten years later, in 1871, some 65,980 souls. Advance like this is only excelled in the mushroom cities of America. Eighty years ago Man- chester with Salford numbered but 24,867 inhabitants. The cotton industry was just then quickening into that vigorous life whose development has contributed so much to the 'prosperity cf the country generally. The hamlets of Lan- cashire expanded into towns, and Manchester was soon the flourishing commercittl capital of the county. The ex- ceeding rapidity with which this important city has extended her borders may be realised when we state that the population of Manchester and Salford in 1861 had in- creased to 441,171, having increased its population during the present century nearly seventeenfold. In 1871 the population returns were—Salford, 124,805; Manchester, 355,665; or a total of 480,470. The increase in population not only in Mapchester and Salford, but in most Lancashire towns, from say 1820 to 1845, was extraordinary. In 1820 the cotton trade advanced by leaps and bounds. In nine years the quantity of raw cotton sent from Liverpool to Manchester had increased by 50,000,000 lbs. weight, and other raw materials had also increased in an almost equal , ratio. In 1830 the Manchester and Liverpool line was opened, and the railway system thenceafter rapidly ex-1 tended, and aided wonderfully in the work of commercial development. All this time the population was very rapidly increasing in all Lancashire towns. Between 1801 and 1861 Preston and Burnley increased their populations sixfold, and during the first 60 years of the nineteenth century Black- burn and Liverpool quintupled their respective populations. Amongst other towns Wigan and Oldham trebled their populations. The most notable iacrease in population in this county between 1861 and 1871 was at Barrow. In the former year, when Barrow merely formed part of the parish of Dalton-in-Farness, and had no separate mention, the population was estimated at 3,300, and in the latter it regis- tered 17,992. The rush to this north-western El Dorado was great, and the town flourished during the years of Lanca- shire's prosperity. The population, it is believed, will not show any material increase on last return. Respecting the population generally during the years 1801 to 1831, the rate of increase was more than twice as fast as that shown by the returns from 1831 to 1861. It was at the rate of from two to three millions every ten years. The reason of this was in a great measure due to the wholesale emigration that took place during the decennial period ending with 1841, consequent on the famine in Ireland. There was also emi- gration on a somewhat large scale in 1846-7. The system of registration under a registrar-general, which was estab- lished in England in 1836, has given considerable assistance in the work by supplying a staff for carrying out the enu- meration, and also by affording the means of checking the census. A similar registration system was extended to Scot- land in 1854, of which the census of 1861 and 1871 has had the advantage. The census of 1851 was taken for the night of the 31st of March; that for 1801 for the night of Sun- day, 7th April; that of 1871 for the night of Sunday, the 2nd of April. Although the Acts of Parliament-43 and 44 Victoria. chap. 37, for England and Wales—under ',which the census is taken provides that certain penalties shall be imposed on persons refusing to fill up schedules, it may reasonably be expected that the forthcoming census will be distinguished, as was that of 1861, by the fact that not a single fine was in- flicted under the penal clauses of the Act. If the head of the family discovers that any entries in the schedule are wrong, he has authority to rectify them; if, for instance, his servants have represented themselves as being more youthful than they really are, he may make any alteration needed to secure accuracy. He has the same power also in the case of his own daughters or other ladies who may be residing in his house at the time, and, if circumstances re- quire, he may add a few years to the ages which they have represented themselves to be—that is, if he dare. lihe in' I formation contained in the schedules will, be considered en- tirely confidential; still, it is not difficult to understand the delicacy and reluctance which some persons in country places may feel in filling up a return which they know will come' under the observation of a neighbour engaged in taking the census in that locality. At the last census fourteen persons, chiefly spinsters, in order to prevent certain information be- coming known to the enumerators, forwarded their schedules direct to the Registrar-General, which irregularity was con- doned in several instances. One of the cases which were condoned was that of a wealthy spinster, of uncertain age. who, not content with fastening the doors of her residence in order to prevent the enumerator from gaining admission, barricaded her windows as if she expected to be besieged, and declared that not even a tine of £2O should induce her to give the required particulars. These facts becoming known at head-quarters, a letter was addressed to the lady which had the effect of soothing the feelings excited by a demand that she should give her age and furnish other in regarding herself, and led her to forward her ichedule to the Registrar-Cieneral- T'IPW.e Were, other in- stances, many of them of an amusing character, in which similar objection was felt, butin most of them the enumera- tors were able, by a courteous explanation and a pledge of secrecy, to perariade the persons no objecting that they bad treason to fear any unpleaaaat results from 'the up

THE WEST LAS/WHIR—E.; .B:SIL—WAT BILL —This bill wits read a second time and referred to a select committee.

QUARTER SESSIONS.—Mr. BORLASS gave .notice that on the first favourable opportunity he would move that "In the opinion of this House the time has now arrived when the local administrative business of the courts of quarter sessions should be transferred to representative bodies elected by the ratepayers." Low. TaxarroN.—Mr. HATHEONE gave notice that, as an amendment to Mr. ffarcourt's motion, he would move a resolution that, considering the complicated charactet of the present system of local taxation, it is expedient that the sums paid towards highways and other local burdens should be investigated by a select committee or a royal commission., ENGLAND, FRANCE, AND TIINIS.—In reply to Mr. Rylands, Sir C. DILEE said that it was quite impossible for him to say what documents existed in the French Foreign Office. At the time of the Berlin Congress there was a conversation between Lord Salisbury and M. Waddington with respect to Tunis, but Lord Salisbury demurred to the interpretation put upon it by M. Waddington, and he did not think that any good would come from re-opening the question.' SERVING A PRISONER WITH A WRIT FOR RENT.-4r. FORSTER, answering Mr. Sexton on the subject of the serving a writ for rent upon Patrick Fevoy while a prisoner in Kilmainham, said that facilities were given for he serving of the writ. The Government did not think that a man should be saved from notice becouse he was detained under the Protection of Person end Property Act, and they wished as far as possible also that he should not stiffer in any civil proceedings he might have to take against others. THE BASUTO Wart.—fn answer to Sir W. Lawson, Mr. Gnaw DUFF said he believed it was the case that there had been renewed fighting in Basutoland. THE WITHDRAWAL FROM CANDAHAR.—REDIViDg IO ques- tions, the Marquis of HARTINGTON said the Information he had was that 4,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry had left ,Cabul for Candalutr. He was not aware whether it was in- tended that this force should be followed by others. Tile cavalry were timed to reach Candahar in 12 days from the time they started, and the infantry would reach four days after the cavalry. _ .

• THE MUTINY BILL.—THB ABOLITION OF FLOGGING.— Mr. OsBORNE MORGAN, in moving the second reading of the Army Discipline and Regulation (Annual) Bill, thought it undesirable that so important a change in military legisla- tion should be presented to the House for the first' time withoht some explanation, particularly with refere Ice to the abolition of the lash and the substitution of other punishments. Corporal punishment had been condemned by public opinion, and in the opinion of military authorities it was not, as at present limited, worth keeping. It must be remembered that ours was a voluntary army, the recruit- ing power fwhich -must depend upon its popularity; and in the belief of many competent judges the lash kept the hest class of men out of the service. When in 1868, a pro- pos-1 was made, as an amendment to the Ninthly Bill, that flogging sheuld be abolished, it was predicted that the effect 'of such a change would be that the army would degenerate :into an armed mob, and that other punishments would enormously Increase; but experience had proved that the limitation of that degrading punishment had been'accom- :panied by a remerkable diminution of other punishments, and there could be no doubt that the soldier of the present day teas a very different man. to the soldier of the past. 'A coward could not be made more courageous by flogging, nor could treachery before the enemy be prevented by the fear of the lash. Drunkenness on the march, and crimes arising out of drunkenness, would be appropriately punished by the lash, but by the Act of 1879 they were precluded front re- sorting to it in those cases, and there was no longer, there- fore, any ground upon which the retention of corporal punishment could be defended. After the Act of 1879, there were three courses open to the Government. They might have left things as they were, but that, under present cir- cumstances, they considered impossible; they might, in the second place, as in the case of the navy, simply abolish cor- poral punishment, without providing a substitute; but if they had done that, they would have done what no other army in the world had done. The third course was that which had been adopted in this bill, namely, the abolition of corporal punishment,, and the provision et ether descrip- tions of summary punishment approved by the highest military authorit(es, and to be administered under rules which, as they might have to he modified by experience, i, was thought better not to embody in the Act. He hoped that those punishments would, like flogging, become rarer and rarer; but they could only hope to reduce the painfully heavy punishment list of the army by raising the morals of the soldier, by removing temptations to drunkenness, by raising the character and states of non-commissioned officers, by cultivating the self-respect of the soldier, and by giving him something to live for and to hope for.—Colonel STAN- MET feared the alocilition of flogging might make it necessary for the punishment of death to be more frequently resorted to. It was not his intention at that stage of the bill to offer any opposition to it. If the Government were satisfied that they could keep up the discipline of the service in the manner they proposed, so much the better, but the resporsibility must rest with them. Mr. Pommes was grateful to the Government for having dealt with the question boldly, and in a manner that he be- lieved would tie satiefactory to the countryit large.--edr W. BaerrreLor could not but excla' im "How. are the mighty fallen ! " when he raw the member for Burnley so meek and submissive. If the late Secretary for War bad proposed one tittle of what was proposed by the present Government, words could not have expressed his abhorrence; bat now be was "gentle as a sucking dove."—Sir H. HAVELOCK ALLEN retained the opinion that corporal punishment was appro- priate for drunkenness bathe face of the enemy and maraud- ing, but, it having been abolished for offences of that kind, there was no longer any ground for its retention.—Sir J. Hat was under the impression that before long, though the t3ecretsry of State might not find it necessary to incrodnoe. the thumb-screw or the booty corporal punishment would have to be restored..,-Mr. Bnamattear, !having served for. some time as a private soldier,'vrae able tO say that there was a detestion of corporal punishment, not ,merely among the men likely to suffer from it, but by every one else. Private isoldiers in England occupied a different position to those of any other country, as it was a disgrace to wear the uniform• of the Queen. The abolition of flogging would raise the character of the men, while its retention was worse than useless, for with the good man it roused feelings of revenge, and the bad Man had better be turned out of the service.— Captain MAXWELL held that it was impossible to raise the moral tone of the soldier so 'long as corporal punishment existed.—Sir A. GORDON coniLmned flogging, but doubted the efficacy of the substituted punishment.—Mr. Orwee rejoiced that the British soldier was at length to be relieved from a degradation to which the soldier el no other country was subjected.—Mr. HOPWOOD was proud. of the triumph' this bill represented of civil over militarropinions.—Mr, CHILDERS said the Government would welcome any suggese tion for the improvement of the substitute punishments.— The bill was read a second time. Tim HIGHWAY ACTS.—Mr. HARCOURT moved that, in the opinion of the' House, it. was expedient so to amend the Highway Act of 1878 that part of the maintenance of main toads might be defrayed from other sources Ilan county rates.—After a long debate, the motion was lost by a vote- -159 against 145. Catensnatt.—Lord WAYENEY inquired whether the Indian or the Afghan Government received at present the revenues of Candahar, and subject to what; also, in the event of Candahar being transferred to the Government of Abdiarrah- man, what means of protection for British bubjects would be adopted, and whether a Consul, withei right of flag and" escort, would reside in the city ?.-Lord ENFIELD was net able to reply specifically to the question asked, but believed that the Indian Government would receive the revenue of Candahar at present. Means would be taken to protect the THE FOOT AND interests of British subjects in that city. ICIOtrTR DISEAsE.—The marquis of Lane of fethLoe Privy vy c Presidentoune lo with, thhe, regard towr e towr dee% thew liintEena relative to the foot and mouth disease which expire on the IllstMarch, and whether the Privy Council had decided what regulations they intended to impose for to the next few months.—Earl SPENCER said the laws passed the YrivY Council for the suppression and prevention of foot and mouth disease were of a very stringent kind, and had been attended ' with results upon which they might congratulate themselves. It was not proposed to revew the old • orders which expired on the 31st March, as it would be impossible to do so at this liM3 of the year, when farmers were compelled te m about from one market to another to buy stock. The order v which regulated the sale of animals in thegreat metroiAntall markets, it was proposed to renew in the same ternv. as be- fore. He was glad to say the efforts of the Privy Council Lo reduce the area of the disease had been attended with great success, as the number of cattle attacked had diminished steadily. The rrivy Council 9119 contemplated issuing Lid- ditional orders for the more effectual isolation of foreign cattle, which they thought would reduce still further the cases of infection. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,, APRA 2, .10111'

TEE WAR wris THE BOgns.—Mr,, Go= gave notice that on the earliest possible opportunity he would move the following resolution :—" That in the opinion, of this House it was not justifiable for Her Majesty's Government to wage war agains:. the Boers for the purpose of obtaining the objects effected by the arrangements now concluded." (Cheers and laughter.) VACCINATION.—Mr. HIBBERT, replying to Mr. P. A. Taylor, said it was ngt a common practice, he was informed, to inoculate the calf with the virus of smallpox: The Local Government Board had no statistics as to the mortality from smallpox in Belgium, but in Holland it was, during the epidemics of 1871 and 1872, very large. There was nothing, however, to show what proportion of cases were vaccinated persons, and it must be borne in mind that neither in Bel- gium nor in Holland watt vaccination Compulsory. There was no intention to introduce a bill for the abolition of com- pulsory vaccination. (Hear, bear.) SURRENDER OF POTCHTLFSTROOII.—In reply to Sir John Hay, Mr. CHILDER3 read the telegram from Sir E. Wood announced in the House of Lords, and observed—lmmedi- ately on receipt of this telegram I conferred with Lord' Kimberley, but we are not yet in possession of sufficient in- formation to guide Her Majesty's Government as to the reply to be sent to Sir E. Wood. I may remind the right honourable baronet that a question may arise as to whether the news of the prolongation of the armistice could have reached Potchefstroorn before March 21; but on this point I express no opinion at present.—Sir S. NownccrrE asked whether it could have reedited there if it had been sent through the Orange Free State P—Mr. CHILDERS : As to that I have consulted those acquainted with the locality,l and I hope that I may not be pressed to say more at present. THE DECIMAL SYSTEM. —4 Mr. ASIrrON DILEE moved that, in the opinion of the House, the introduction of the decimal system of coinage, weights, and measures ought not to be longer delayed.—Mr. Du:yens seconded the motion. STEVENSON, in opposing the motion, said there had been no such demand for the adoption of the decimal system as would justify the House in agreeing to the resolution before it.—Mr. ANDERSON moved as an amendment that the question be referred to a Select Committee.—Mr. HUBBARD argued that decimals were all very well as a scientific exer- cise, but would be of no real practical 1190.—Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN trusted the motion would not be pressed, and that the movers of both the motion and the amendment would be content with having called attention to the subject, and not press the question to a diviaien.—Mr. DILEE said he should not press his motion, but would withdraw it in favour of the amendment of the honourable member for Glasgow. Mr. GLADSTONE said the practical question had consequently become' this—whether there was a case for sending the matter to a select committee or not. As for himself he had always, when Chancellor of the Exchequer, objected, not to a decimal system, but to the introduction of any chinge that did away with the penny, which was the basis of the cash transaction of the country; and, as far as this went, he thought the House was already sufficiently possessed of the facts, and that no sufficient reasons had been given to in- duce that already overcharged assembly, which had now got through one,half of the session, to appoint a select com- mittee on a question that had so often been inquired into.— The House divided, and the motion having been negatived, the amendment was put with the following result :—For the amendment., 28; against, 108. SALE OF BENEFier.a.—Mr. H. LEATHAM called attention to the evidence of the Royal Commission on the Sale of Benefices, from which he read numerous extracts, and moved a resolution declaring that the simoniacal evasion of the law, and other scandals connected with the exercise and dis- posal of private patronage in the Church of England, call for remedial measures of the most stringent and radical cha- racter.—Mr. STUART WORTLEY, thinking the language of the resolution stronger than was justifiable, moved as an ainendrrient that the report discloses evils which call for legislation at the earliest possible moment.—Mr. J. G. TALBOT seconded the amendment.—Mr. GLADSTONE, while remarking on the slight difference between the amendment and the motion and on the practical unanimity on both sides on the subject, said that it was impossible to overrate'the demoralising effect of these transactions on the olergy con- cerned. At the same time he Pointed .out that the number of them was comparatively limited. As to the Government taking up the question, it was impossible for them to do that without displacing some other question; and before giving any undertaking on the subject be thought the House should 'have an opportunity of discussing the bill which Mr. E. Stanhope had brought in. He expressed a hope, there- fore, that the House would not be called on to pronounce an opinion now.—The amendment and the motion were then both withdrawn. . , HOUSE OF,COMMONS.--WEDNESDLI.

SLAVERY IN THB TRANSVAAL.—Sir Wilfred Lawson gave notice that when Mr. R. N. Fowler put his question with respect to the observance of the Sand River Convention, pro- hibiting slavery north of the Vaal River, he would further ask if the Government could give any information with respect to the number of slaves within the Transvaal terri- tory, and what course her Majesty's Government intended to adopt in reference to them. OPEN SPACES IN LONDON.—Mr. W. H. James moved the Second reading of the Metropolitan Open Spaces Act (18T7) Amendment Bill. . He pointed out that the act in question had not realised the hopes of its . promoters, and it was desirable to extend the facilities by which the squares, pri- vate gardens, and 'disused burial grounds for public benefit. ' Whenever any large space became available there was'great anxiety manifested to secure it for public use,. but these efforts failed for want of proper facilities, and the object of his bill was to provide that a majority of two-thirds of those interested in the squares, dec., should transfer them to the Metropolitan Board of Works or the District Vestry, and he was quite willing to entertain any proposal for compensation for the rights of those parties who objected to such transfers.— Earl FBRCY moved the rejection of the bill, arguing that it was unjust and inequitable to deprive the tenants and owners of property in the equareaand open spaces of the metropolis of the 'right's they 'had. hitherto possessed. Viscount FOLKESTONE seconded-the' amendment. Mr. WHITLEY trusted Eirt Percy-Would consent to waive his opposition to this stage of the bill. From experience among the very large I constituency he represented; he knew. hoe/ essential it was to preserve these open spaces; and in regard to church- yards, the city which, he represented had done much in beautifying them, and making them valuable for the use of the public, • kle assumed that the honourable member who moved the second reading of the bill would be willing to agree to the introduction of' a clause to afford compensation for those whose, Interests might be affected.'-Mt. dottRT- STEY, On the part of the Clove' nment, approved the object of the bill, and promised it support if compensation clauses were introduced.—Mr. JAMES promised that such clauses ' should be introduced.—Earl Pnricir withdrew his opposition and the bill was read a second time. Huse citrus DISEASES (IRELAND) BILL.---Mr. GRAY moved the second reading of the Infectious Diseases (Ire- land) Bill, explaining that it simply provided that under certain conditions information was to be given to the sani- tary authorities in Ireland of the outbreak of infectious dis- eases: The bill Was to be read in connection with the Public Health Act, and gave no new powers affecting individuals beyond the Detification of infectious disorders.—The Sotacrrou-GENERAL for IRELAND said the Government did not oppose Cie measure, and it was read a second time. PUBLIC•HOLISES AND ELECTION DAM—Mr. CARBUTT moved the second reacting of the Elections (Closing of Public-houses) Bill, the object of which -was that public- houses should be closed on election dais. The honourable gentleman gave instancerin which the experiment of closing. the public-houses had been tried on days of election with marked benefit to the localities, and urged that compulsory. closing all over the kingdom would ensure greater quiet and freedom from riotous proceedings. In the town of Knitres- borough, where there was a small number of voters and a large number of public-houses, one of the constituents whose condition on an 'election day bespoke of frequent atten- dance or the licensed victuallers, was asked if he could tell how many public-houses he had been into, and his reply, after an endeavour to recollect, was, in Yorkshire parlance, that he was "fair 'capped."—Mr. Lrrrox supported the bill,, bet moved the adjournment of the debate, in order-to afford time to take the opinion of the licensed victuallers on the sub.. ject.—Baron DE FERRIERS seconded the amendmend.—Mr. MORGAN LLOYD supported the measure, aud stated that there was a straug feeling in its favour throughout South Wales.-*The ATTORNEY-GENERAL hoped the bill would not be pressed to a division that day, but that those who had charge of the measure would consent to the adjournment of the debate, in order that the question might be further con- sidered pending the discussion of the Corrupt Practices Bill. 7-Sir it. CRQSS hoped the promoters of the bill would accept the advice of the Attorney-General.—Mr. CAINE supported the principle of the meaeure, hat expressed a hope that tne motion for adjournment would be assented to.—Sir W. Lew- SON urged that the bill should be pressed to a division, and if it:were tread a second title the Government would be fortified by the vote of the House in bringing forward the Corrupt Practices Prevention .Bill.—Mr. CARBLITT assentecl to the motion for adjournment, and it was agreed to. -EXTENSION OF CORPORATE BOUNDARIES.—Mr. W. Fow- rntt moved the second reading of the Municipal Corporation Act (ItS5B) Amendment Bill, the object of which was to avoid the expense of coming to Parliament for power to en- large municipal boundaries by vesting the necessary author- ity in the Board of Trade.:--Mr. Couirrtrev assented to the bill on behalf of the Government, and it was read a second time.
