HARCOURT declared, amidst the cheers of the House, that the •article In. that journal on- which pro- one-dings bad beeti-ake-n was a "donOestio crime," and that the crpvernment would not have done its dnty if ,it had not Instituted the prosecution. He had taken the proceedings, on his own responsibility, and had had no instigation what-,, ever from any foreign Power.—Mr. GLansrosn answered a question-, as to the "profit" which had been or might be made oethe Suez Canal shares purchased by Lord Beacons- field's Government. The shares bear no interest coupons until 1894, but in the meantime we receive 5 per cent. on the purchase money from the Khedive, and if the shares were sold no doubt a large profit could be realised. ARMY DISCITLINS BILL.—On the motion for going into cornnaittee upon the Mutiny Bill, at amendment by Viscount Emlyn on the subject of discipline in the army led to a renewed discussion on corporal punishment. The amend- ment was withdrawn, and the House went into committee. Debate on a proposal 14 Mr. Caine to stop the supply of intoxicating liquors at canteens followed, but the proposal was rejected, on a division, by 156 against 34.
EXTRA ORDIWY BIZEACII OF PRMSE CASE.

A SHIRTLESS VISCOUNT. • : In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, before Mr. , Justice Stephen and-a Lomeram jury, the case Nolf v. Garden , was heard. This was an action for breach of premise of marriage, and also to recover £35 for money lent. The de- fendant who did not appear either in person or by counsel, pleaded a number of pleas, one being that be was obliged to marry another lady because the plaintiff unnecessarily absented and secreted herself from him. Mr. Douglas Kingsford, who appeared for the plaintiff, said she was the daughter of a marble merchant at Forest- gate, Essex, and that the defendant was been de Garden; a Belgian viscount, who occupied a very romantic and peculiar position. In 1877, when the plaintiff was 20 years of age, the defendant agreed to marry her, representing himsel f to be a poet and a dramatic author, who, in a short time wofild earn 3,000 francs a month, and also come into his ancestral estates. With these prospects he led the plaintiff to believe that be would be able to marry her and keep her in good style. Among his numerous letters to the plaintiff, was one beginning darling," and ending with this passage, "I have bought a new shirt. It is so. I could not do otherwise. Remember that the Vincent a. Chateau- briand, the great French writer, also was in the same posi- tion. Chateaubriand had only one shirt, and he washed it himself, and he wrote splendid novels and he became a Minister." The next communication was in the shape of a telegram to the plaintiff, in which he said, " Lostomleas send £2 15s. before twelve to-morrow." In a subsequent letter he said, "If £1 is sent to-morrow, telegraph before six o'clock. I can start at night, otherwise I could not. lam exhausted, but, darling, be assured I love you dearly." In another he told her that he had been starving, and that having no food he was obliged to sell the very shirt he bought the day before. Then he added, "You told me that you would send me something. I have been waiting. I am not a man receiving money from a woman, and I would be sorry to turn such a one, but as I have no one to help, I accept what you do as a fait d'honneur, as we say in French." There were other applications for money on the grouhd that he was starving, but he held out hopes that his dramatic efforts in Paris would be successful, and that he would get 1,000 francs a night for each of his plays. in one letter he wrote, "I have not eaten anything since yesterday mid-day, and lam obliged to sell my last shirt to a mer- chant on the Vieux Marche, in order to get food—that is to say, some bread. I have sold all my shirts, and I have been living on bread and water for a fortnight, except the days I had nothing at all." To meet his wants the plaintiff sold jewellery and other property belonging to her, and, in all advanced him £35, which she now sought to recover. Ulti- mately, he promised to send her, in a parcel, a letter written in invisible or sympathetic ink, telling her where they should meet for the purpose of being married, but the parcel never came, and in 1879 lie married another lady in London and wrs new abroad. The plaintiff, who was called, said she first met the defen- dant in Brussels, and that her father had advanced him money to carry on a newspaper. She had never seen or heard from the defendant since he promised to send her a letter in invisible ink. Mr. Justice Stephen, in Summing up, said the plaintiff was clearly entitled to the £35, and whatever damages the jury thought she ha e sustained by the defendant failing te carry out his promise, but he could not think they were innch if his story was true that he had been compelled to sell his shirts. The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff for £3OO, in- cluding the £35. ' His Lordship said he hoped the plaintiff would get the ' money. .

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The secretary of the 'Fife and Clackrnannan Miners Association has received from the Lord-Advocate the expres- sion of his opinion that it is illegal for coalowners to enforce conditions of employment, such as stipulating for deduc- tions from wages, conditions of residence dm. The ironworkers employed by the largest firm in Burnley have received an intimation that on Saturday there will be paid an advance of 2s. per week tø mechanics and Is. per week to labourers. This amount was deducted from the the men's wages over two years ago. At the meeting of the amalgamated committee appointed by the Rossendale cotton operatives, on Tuesday, the ques- tion of considering what steps to pursue in order to obtain an advance on the present rate of wages was considered at great length. A large number of operatives were also pre- sent, and the following resolution was passed:—" That in the opinion of this meeting it is inexpedient to continue the agitation for the present, but that we take the earliest oppor- tunity that a further revival of trade may produce to bring our case again before the manufacturers, and we trust with better results than have attended our last efforts." The agitation in favour of a large union of cotton operatives is still going on, and the general opinion is that one will shortly he formed. _ _ _

On 'Wednesday, a large hody of miners, formerly employed at Darfield Main Colliery, Barnsley, signed new contracts at the old rate of wages, with slight alterations. This is the only idle colliery which was closed when the great strike began. One serious result of the struggle bas been the banishment of trade from the district. This week the colliers will only work three daye;whilst prices are now lower than for some time past.

Over 1,600 emigrants arrived in New York on Monday. If a man would take care of his health he must take air. ,Epitaph for a Tramcar Conductor.—He took his last fare well. There is one thing that every man puts off from day to day, and that is his necktie. Could it be said of the man who rang the bell for a false alarm of fire that he tolled a lie. "Well, friend, as thee hest sworn, thee may do it, but, thee must not make a prac- tice of it." Richard Earnest Cooke, of the well-known firm of John Cooke and Son, stock and share brokers, Bradford, has filed a petition with liabilities estimated at £82000., and assets not I yet ascertained. The failure has caused some excitement in I Bradford. The young milkman and his betrothed stood before the registrar of marri ages. if that was the only whey. The editor of a Wineonsin paper says," Wednesday's mail brought to us a letter addressed 'Rev.' another, 'The Hon.,' another 'Col.,' one 'Mr.,' and the last 'Esq.' On the way to dinner we accidently stepped on a woman's train, and she ad- dressed us thus—' You brute !'" New rates were granted at Ashton-under-Lvne, on Wed- nesday, when it was stated that the amount? applied for were lower than had been asked for at any time within the last 30 or 40 years.

It is laid that the costs of the plaintiff in the case of Lawson v. Labouchere hare amounted to over £3OO a day. Those of Mr. Labouchere would be much less, but still con- siderable, as he made himself responsible for the defence of the printer. The disagreement of the- jury bad been ex- pected from the first in Westminster Hall, and it is reported that they were seven to five, though acconuts differ with respect to what view was taken by the majority. A Liberal banquet was held at Gravesend on Wednesday to celebrate the return of Sir Sydney Waterlow for the borough.—Sir Thomas Chambers, responding for the House of Commons, dwelt strongly on the obstructien recently. carried (id,' and said he believed the coercion measure adopted would be for the substantial benefit of the well-disposed and honest people of Ireland.—Professor Rogers, in responding for the Government in the absence of any member of the Ministry, defended the action of Mr. Gladstone's Govern- ment as in the highest degree beneficial to the country. • Mr. Cdffard, judge of the Halifax County Court, has had before him a claim of £44 4s. for damages, the action being , brought by Jonathan Marsden, tenant of Kirklees Farm, against Messrs. Webb and Co., tar distillers, of Brighouse, Damage was alleged to have been done last year to growing crops to the amount of £36 6s. by gases from the defendants' works, the rest of the claim consisting of valuers' charges and other expenses. A verdict was given for £2O 65., with costs. THE TITRE QUESTION IN WA,LES. Recently several largely attended and enthusiastic meetings have been held in villages in the neighbourhood of Mold to discuss the tithe question. The meetings have been addressed by the Rev. J. Eiddim Jones (Llanrug), one of the agents of the Liberation Society, ao well as by several tenant farmers from the neighbourhood. Resolutions were unanimously' carried, to the effect "that the tithes should be devoted to national purposes, such as the payment of the poor, high- way, and education rates." The farmers themselves origi- nated the meetings, and an organisation has been formeds amongst them for the purpose of discussing the question, which is at present receiving their close attention, and for bringing it to a speedy settlement. Mr. Gladstone's letter concerning the tobacco duty has, perhaps;by the appearance it has of Ininimising the surplus at his control, tended to diminieh curious expectations as to. the forthcoming Budget. It is now very generally thought that the Chancellor of the Exchequer will announce on Mon- day s new scale ef charges for telegrams in the direction of, the change of price set forth by Mr. Fawcett in one or two of his speeches since he has been at the Post-office. The least, agreeable part of Mr. Gladstone's statement will probably be iri connection with further expenses for the Transvaal war. It is now supposed that the amount included in the Army, and Navy Estimates for 1881-2 will be adequate to meet the cost that has already been incurred. But as the expenditure cannot yet be regarded as concluded, it is not yet certain that the matter will not be left to be dealt with by-supplementary.estimates at a much later period of the year. • It is said by those whose opinion must be regarded as of great authority that if anyone will take the trouble to read the first 92 pages of the yolumne which the Cobden Club have been induced by Mr. Gladstone to republish he will ob- tain a fair cmception of the Government Land Bill for Ire- land, and it is even added that the only point upon which he will lack information will be as to where the money is to be found by -means of which the' purchase of holdings in Ireland is - to' Tit 'prombted. This is a con= sideration which will occupy an important place in the exposition of the measure on April 7. It is said that the remnant of the Church Serplus Fund will figure in that statement, that it is .larger than has been supposed; that it fully amounts to the sum anticipated in Mr. Glad= stone speeches upon the policy of disendowment of the Church of eland in 1809, end that in bid skilful hands a command of money amounting to not less than £4,000,000 might in this way be obtained. Mr. Gladstone is the author of the suggestion .that this fund should be devoted exclu- eively to the relief of unavoidable suffering, and it is bel lieved he will contend that the circumstances of land tenure in Ireland fully justify the employment of the Church sur- plus in that direction. The definition of the Ulster Custom, and the extension of the "three V's" to all Ireland, are practically though not precisely adopted in the dovernment Bill. &me points will and must be left to be worked out by practice in the new land tribunal. But of Mr. Gladstone's view as to the obstacles which kayo impeded the operation of the Bright clauses there can be no doubt. It is under- stood that in suggesting the republication of the volume referred to Mt. Gladstone had given particular attention to the followingpassage :—" The principal laws that prevent that frequent transfer of land which Would put an,end to absenteeism are the law of primogeniture, the heavy stamp duty on conveyance, the law which permits property to be settled on unborn persons, and the general complications permitted ia the titles to real property. Something has been done to facilitate the transfer of hind ly the creation of the Landed Estates Court, but it is an inconvenient anomaly and exhibits the imperfection of the law that a lawsuit should be thought the best and the most expeditious mode of selling an estate. The Record of Title Act has been passed to facilitate further the transfer of land, but it has not been very effective, and as bug as settlernents are permitted the transfer of land cannot be free from difficulty."'

FRlDAY.—Before His Worship the Mayor .I.a.rries Harrison Esq,) and Mr. E. Johnson. - AFTER THE FuNanAt.—Patriok Carney was charged with assaulting Mary Carney, his wife; on Sunday.—Complainant said that on the day in question her husband had been with a funeral to the cemetery, and on comiag home he called her all sorts of names. She did not say anything in return, , and he continued in that way all day. At night they both I went to the house from which the funeral started, and whilst 1 there he abused her and pulled from her head the hair pro- duced. At her request a man named Dennis Kelly put her husband out of the house.—Mr. Swift (who appeared for defendant): When you got home that night your husband Vie in bed.—Witness admitted that and said that she carried four chairs and a table out of the house while her husband was in bed. She had one of her husbands watches, and had in her possession a pawaticket in respect of another.—Mr. Swift said there had .been a funeral, and they were making merry drinking, and this little scrimmage only took place about ten o'clock, and after her husband had gone she stayed to finish her jollification at Derkin's. -Then she went home and finding her huFband in bed, cleared the house, and went to the court and laid information for an assault.—Mr. John- son: But what about this hair ?—Mr. Swift :Os, a woman combs hair out of her head every morning.- You never knew an IrisliWoman come here without a bundle of hair. (Laughter.) Nobody pretends the woman was hurt, and she admitted herself that she has came here to get maintenance for herself and child. The fact is she likes somebody die better than her husband, and she exhibits her baby as being mere like a better mats than her husband. 1 have a witness here svbn can prove it..—The Beach thought there was fault on both sides, and dismissed the case.

MONDAT.—Before Messrs. H. A. Bright and Willis. AssAuLTING THE Pumcn.—George Armstrong was eharged with beinz drank and disorderly in Liverpool-road, and assaulting P.C. Wel!wood, on Saturday night.— Prisoner was creating a disturbance, and on the constable interferinir, prisoner kicked him in the body, in consequence of which he had been under the care of the doctor.—Fined 53. and costs for being drank, or seven clays' imprisonment, and 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for the assault. —William Donoghue, a young lad, was charged with being drunk, and assaulting P.C. Poeble.—Fined ss. and costs, and 10s. and costs, for each charge respectively. A VIOLENT Fattosr.—John Griffiths, employed, at Messrs. Menzies' chemical works, was charged with assaulting his wife, on the lqt May, 1878, and also with assaulting her on the 25th March.—Mr. Bright: How is it this case only comes on to-day F.—Superintendent Johnston: He was away a very long time, but I believe he as been in the town for some time. His wife did not tell us until now, and she isas much afraid of bins over.--Complamant said that prisoner was threatening her Meter; who was in the Mese; and on witness interfering, prisoner threw a chair at her, and also struck her with his fist several times in the face.—Complainant's brother, who witnessed the assault, corroborated the above statement, and prisoner was fined £2O and costs.. BRIDGET'S 108TH APPEARANCE. Bridget Kildare was charged with being drunk and disorderly, on Saturday night, in Liverpeol-road.--Superintendent Johnston caused some sensation in court by announcing that this was prisoner's 108th eppearance at that court, and her 3rd appearance this year.—Bridget told the court as she has done many times on former occasions to "go home and laugh at yersels." —Mr. Bright: I suppose she is the blackest of any on your list P.—Superintendent Johnston: I don't think anybody has been 107 times.—Bridget: Yes, I am locked up if I walk the streets quietly.—She we sent to prison for one month.

A SEPARATION SEVEN MONTHS AFTER MARRIAGE.— Joseph Twist, Eccleston, was charged with being drunk, and assaulting his wife, Ann Twist, at two o'clock, on Sunday morning.—Complainant said she had three children, and had only been married seven months to the prisoner. At the time mentioned prisoner was wanting to fight with his brother. She tried to prevent him from getting to him, and he then comm.nced to abuse her. She did not want to live with him as she was in danger of her life, whether her hus- band was drunk or sober. He had smashed nearly all the things in the house.—Prisoner: She has got her mother with us, and her mother's husband; and if I speak I ant threatened with a warrant.—Complainant: No, Joseph, that is not correct—Prisoner: I will allow her 7s. a week.— Complainant: Very well, I will be agreeable to that.

Not every one can reason as closely about the marriage relation as the negro who said, "I got an old muader, an' if don' buy shoes an' stockings for her she won't have none. Nov, if I get married I would have to buy dem tings for my' wife, and that would look like takin' de shoes and stoCkings right out of my poor ole mudder's" mouf, don' you see?" At Middleton, a shocking case of death from destitution was before the county coroner, Mr. Molesworth. The evi- dence showed that deceased, John Haywood, 67 years of age, was found by.the police in an uno...cupied house. He was in a dreadful condition, his bones protruding through his skin, and being Covered with wounds. He was carried into another house, bat died in a few mintitee. & verdict of "Death from want, cold, and exposure," was returned.. ~A man may be terribly sarcastic and not know it. A prq-- fessor lecturing on chemistry to a class of young men askdd Mr. Jones if prussic acid was at all 'dangerous. Mr. Jon replied that it was rather powerful, and if taken in.sufficie t quantity would destroy life. "Rather powerful ?" sneer the professor.- "Why, Mr. Jones, if I should put a sing 'e drop of it on your tongue it would kill a dor ' Sit Sedgley, James Bodenham, 22, was remanded on a charge of attempting to murder his sweetheart, Lizme Williams, and tor attempted suicide. It is alleged that on Sunday Miss Williams upbraided the accused for his incon- stancy; and this so annoyed him that upon separating he said,"You shall never see me again." A succession off revolver shots followed, causing Williams to be stunned an Bodenham to be injured on the head. Eincrieu. proposed a vote of thanks to the chair- man; this was seconded by Mr. R. %anima, and carried. The Cnannteat said he was very much obliged to them. Anything that he could do to keep things in harmony, he should have very much pleasure in doing. He had been overseer for 12 or 13 years, and everything had passed off very agreeably. He was happy to say they had still their collector and assistant overseer bolding the same situations. He was sure they had never had any occasion to find fault with them, and Mr. Twist had -never bees behind with his accounts. (Hear, hear,) WINDLE RURAL. The annual meeting of the ratepayers of this township was held on Friday afternoon, at the Gerards Arms, Denton's Green. Tnere were presar Messrs. H. S. Hall, Arkwrigtit, James Sephton, Hal-ion, Richard Garnett. Little, William Ashcroft, J. Sephton, Joseph Robinson, Richard Unsworth and William Tyrer.

Mr. Hall was elected to the chair, lie said they had not got a very blooming state of affairs to present to them, but still it was better than he anticipated. There had been a good deal of work for the surveyor this year; and a great deal of extra work and trouble had been iniposed upon him by the new system of bookkeeping which the Government bad introduced. He (the chairman) had had two or three hours with the books an the previous evening, and he thought it was making work to a considerable extent in a small parish like that. They began the year with a balance Of £52 12s. lid.; but he ought to say that they did not pay close up that last year. The fact was there was not money to pay all bills, and another thing there was a eumof money owing from the family of the late surveyor, and that money had not been got in, and although there appeared to be £52 there was nothing really in hand. lie Walfl' happy to say however, that the money had been paid n part, the rest . was not doubtful, and their surveyors, Mr. Pye and Mr. Swift, were treating the matter as if if were perfectly good. Mr. Swift :.1 have received £lO of that to-day. Mr. Hall was very happy to hear that. They had since raised in rates £329 16s. 3d.,and only 10s: sd. was put down as doubtful arrears. During the past year £ll ss. 10d. had been considered as bad chiefly arising from property not being tenanted. He was gm ite satisfied Mr. Swift had done the best he could. Of course, they could not get money from empty Louses. They had also received £lO from the Bridgemaster for the county bridges. The expenditure this year had been: Manual labour, £lou 12s. lid.; team labour, .£136 Is. 85.; materials, £135 Bs. 80.; tradesmen's bills and miscellaneous, £4 12s. 2d.; t0ta1,.£.385 15s. sd, The cost of manual labour the previous year was £ll4 7s. Od. ; team labour, £lOO 17s 3d materials were not paid for last year, except, £25 16s. t3d. Incident expenses amounted to £3l, but that included a portion of the salary of the late surveyor. They had now to settle about the salary of their surveyor. Last year he was not paid anything at all, although be had to do the work. There was no money to pay with, and that matter was allowed to be in abeyance. So far as his experience vent there bad been a great deal of work, and if any of them liked to go through the books they would find that it was so. He dared say they would know what Mr. Swift bad done in respect of the work of the roads better than be did, and they were for- tunate in having such a good man for the position. It was held out to him that he would receive £4O, and if the work was done well they used to give a bonus of £5., The Govern- ment would not agree to that. All the money must be given in the shape of a salary. Messrs. John Pye, and William Swift were reappointed surveyors, the latter receiving £4O as working surveyor. £l5 was voted to him as part salary of last year, and this twuirteh tt3e y3sea.4rdt.uallinsc3idlesTl9mex.penses brought the expendi- __ _ -

MITE. Mr. SwiFr said if they only had a 101. rate this year they would probably require an extra one. If they got Denton's Green-lane made into a main road, they would be able to carry on their affairs with a 10d. rate as before. It AVM a pleasure to him to have a man like Mr. Swift as surveyor. He could see whdt an interest he took in the work, and it was very desk- abld they should have a man of substance and intelligence for the post. He had very little 'doubt thiey would have better roads and get more work done for their money before long.

_ The first annual general meeting of this society was held oir Wednesday, in the• Assembly-room of the Fleece Hotel, Mr. Thomas Sherlock presiding. Thu° were a good many members present.

BALANCE SHEET. The Climaxes/ read the balance sheet, and congratulated the members on the very satisfactory .condition of the society. The result of the year's workinecould not but be gratifying to all concerned, inasmuch as there was a balance in favour of the society of £54 14s. 8,1. The income of the society for the year had been : --From subscaiptions, £1,268 33.; entrance foes, £5B; entrance fees forfeited, £1 65.; transfer fees, ss. (Id.; -tranafero of appropriations, £l4; fines on subscriptions, £7 14s. Id.; tines on -repar runts, gd, ; bank interest, £3 Is. id. ; sub- scriptions forfeited, 4s. Bd. ; sale of subscription repayments of appropriations, £415 rule books, kn., £23 s. ; d 13s. 4d.; &posit on sale of appropriation by tender, £4; total receipts, .£1,420 19s. The expenditure had been :—By L 950; preliminary. expenses, appropriations, which included carriage, railway printing, advertising, expenses, incorpora- ting rules, rent of room for lecture, gratuity to Mr. Starr (live guineas), £37 10s. 4d.; year's expenses—lent of room for appropriation and subscription meeting; x 6 EN.; sta- tionery and postages,9s.9d. secretary's guarantee premium, ; £1 ss. 13d.; bank commission and cheque book, £1 ss. lid. 4 office rent. £7 directors' fees (less lines), £l5 19s. ; secretary's sala;ry, £45; the safe and stand, deed; box, balloting • apparatus, rubber stamp, seal, and Money bowls cost £l7 Gs.; books, forms, dm ; I £l2 9s. 6d.; subscription and rule books, £lO 12i. ; paid for oth appropriation £23; cost of sale of appropriation by tender, &c., £1 7s. 6d.; cash in Manchester and Salford bank, £283 15s. 7d.; cash in band £1 45. lid. The advance ac- count showed that £950 had been advanced on five appro- priations; £4O 13s. 4d. had been repaid leaving £909 6s. Bd. owing. The CHAIRMAN said that the preliminary expenses would not occur again. In these societies as in others, the first year was always the most costly. He moved the adoption of the report and balance sheet. Mr. JOSEPH ELLISON seconded the motion which was carried.

TEE DIRECTORS. The meeting then proceeded to elect four directors, the re- tiring ones being, Messrs. Martin, Lowe, Ellison, and Donnelly. The following gentlemen were nominated, and after the voting the result was i—W. G. Ashton, 56; James Appleton, 51 ; Joseph Ellison, 48; H. Martin, 37; Lowe, 22; 11arr,22; Donnelly 20. The four first-named were de- clared duly elected.

div.head: AUDITORS.
div.p: AUDITORS.

The election of auditors was.next proceeded with, Messrs. James Appleton, and Edward A. Robinson having been the auditors for the last year. Mr. James Appleton, having been elected a director, was not eligible for re-dection. The voting on the gentlemen nominated was as follows :—Robinson, 52; T. Crooks, 30; Hopgood, 10; Keillie, 6: Bates, 14. Messrs. Robinson and Crooks were declared elected.

SECRETARY'S SALARY. 'I he secretary's salary (Mr. A. (irilila) was allowed to be the same as last year, namely, £45. Mr. GRIFFIN returned thinks briefly, and said he had always endeavoured to discharge his duties to the utmost.

VOTES OF THANKS. Mr. SKAIFE proposed a vote of thanks to the directors for their services during the past year. He thought they might fairly say the directors bad done the work very well, and if the business was carried on in the future the same as it had been during the past year, the St. Helens Starr-Bowkett Society would have a very successful career. Mr. W. U. ASHTOW seconded the motion, which was carried,and. Mr. Sherlock having replied on beaali the directors, the business terminated, and the first The meeting then closed.,

div.head: ST. HELENS LITERARY AND SCIENTIFIO
div.p: ST. HELENS LITERARY AND SCIEN- TIFIO

The fortnightly meeting of .this Association was held on Tuesday evening, in the Lecture-room, Brook-street. M- R. Pilkington presided, and there was a good attendance. The Rev. H. H. Higgins, MA., read a paper on " Vitalty.'t The paper was devoted to the consideration of some goes- tions bearing upon two propositions of some eminent physio- logists, amongst whom there was a growing tendency to deny, or at all events to question, the existence of vitality as distinct from the action of known forces, such as heat, light, electricity, &c, or something analag,ous to these. The views of those physiologists could be 'briefly stated i—lst. Of the natuie of vitality we know nothing; we are, there- fore, not required either to admit or deny its exigence as a distinct thing. 2nd. The observed phenomena of life are consistent with, and to a very great extent derivable from, the operation of known laws. It is, therefore, not phile- eophical to introduce an entirely unknown agency to ac- count for such residual phenomena as are not thus reducible. The lecturer showed that they could know nothing of the nature of vitality, because it had no analogy 'with any of the known forces. For on this supposition, in what form could knowledge of vitality hold its place in our minds? Not in any of the old familiar forms, such as predicates respecting its quantity, intensity, polarity, and the like; for the thing thue known would have analogy with known forces Lind would not be a thing sui generis, but would fall naturally into some recognised category. This, the lecturer said, did not tell for nor against the probability of its existence: Having noticed the manner in which one group of living things passes into another, he argued that if vitality is analogous to or co-relative with the known forces, we Might expect to all events some resemblance existing between their respective properties and model,ot action; but among the results of the action of heat, electricity, chemical affinity, ike., on various forms of matter, no single instance could be found resembling the commencement of the func- tions of vitality. It was well-known that the common hydra may be produced by a small portion of its body severed from the rest, or even by a small portion of one of its tentacles, which showed that the prototype of the perfect form to be evolved must have been in the particle capable of being thus developed. The prototype of the oak existed in the acorn even to the veins of the leaf. But known forces such as heat, electricity, light, ilic., had no more tendency to produce a leaf than to produce an animal, except from the direction given to their energies by the original iuitium. ~;Dr. McNieote asked if he had excluded altogether in this lecture about vital principal what was ordinarily known as the spirit of mind. He thought it would have been as well to have disclaimed that he had anything to say with regard to the mind of man as he thought that might be hovering about while he was talking about some hidden and mysterious , force outside the forces of matter. He might have dis- claimed that he had no reference to the human mind, or the soul of man ordinarily understood. i The LECTURER thought it would be plain to all that be ' said his whole subject to-night was on what man possessed in COMMQD with a particle of "red snow," and he was talk- ing not only about that which man had in commou with the higher animals, but also with the vegetable and other low forms of vitality. Dr. McNrcom. said they had bad all sorts of subjects there, they had had "beer," and the "dykes of Holland," but now they had something beyond those subjects, which were of a tangible character; mid it was very difficult after hearißg the lecture rapidly read over to see the points and form an opinion on the subject. He should like the lecturer to say —as he did not say what this life was or this vitality; whether he would say• it was in the heavens above or the , earth beneath. (Laughter.) The lecturer had said it was not matter, and it was not the force of matter; well then, did he say that it was the spirit? Was it something which they understood by spiritual nature? He was inclined to think that the principal Wu', tion by most people as Christian men was that this vital: principle was Divine power. Then it was is spirituadagencYl ' and not a nataral one. The lecturer had said that they mt* ' not play fast 'and loose; it had either a natural or a spiritual origin. The lecturer did not say •which it was. if the upshot of the whole lecture was tø luaew nothing of those vistas which were open to tnem as mentioned by the lecturer, and the passages of which led to nowhere, then where were they ? (Laughter.) . The LECTURER said they recognised some things by their position of polarity. some by their weight, and some by their properties. If they were to recognise this same vitality by any of the properties to which he now referred, it would be of ' the nature ef these mechanical forces, which he telieved it was not. A question had been asked by his friend,,the critic—and it was one quite appropriate to the question, and one which he felt no difficulty in answering it. The vital principle was one that was not known, and they must be content with that. And there were more tnings between heaven and earth-of the nature of which they were unable to speak, and of which they were unable to form a description. He should leave them with the impression that he wa,s very orthodox. He knew it was known by a very ugly name—it was called Pantheism—but he believed it was divine life that ran through the whole of nature; net only in living things but in inanimate things, each as the rock, the sea, and the skiet. This divine life pervaded all things. It WaS to him a doctrine which he held dearer than life. It was, he thought, that which they roust in the err; .receive and though not proved, was rationally probable. - The CHAIRMAN said Dr. McNicoll did not seem to be in- clined to take the little crumbs of assistance, but wanted somehow to rush off to make everything right from the top instead of f- :n the bottom. To any religions and careful mind the manner in which Mr. Higgins showed the int- mense gulf between vital principle throughout the world everywhere, the vast difference between life and matter was Wonderful assiktance to a religious mind that faced the diffi- He did not think Dr. McNieoil cult questions of the day. Was sufficiently thankful for that material assistance to a religious mind that approached thanks—not like some shut up recluse, but a mind that boldly faced the difficult gad- Cons of the day. • I Mr. ALLEN pbserved how inductive the lecturer was in ail his processes of reasoninz, and what careful and reverent steps he always took in the introduction. lie believed it was -n the question of the day which all theaiad minds we trying to investigate; Not only itn_thetninde oCtnen' bit in the minds of children there niae th'e question, 'what is life, and why the flour was differtsst fteultntbe:wo9Wad e i:l egg different from a steno? e,• , .. _ The usual votes of thankebreught the theet to einet. . Tun revelations at the recent Election Commissions have, it is grievous to confess, been quite startling in their character. Notwithstanding all that has been said and done to stem the tide of bribery and corrup- tion which deluges a constituency at almost every electiOn it still continues in unabated force. Maccles- field is not the only place which has men upon its Parliamentary register who are willing to sell their ! political privileges for a few shillings or a pot ef beer, but it may fairly challenge comparison with any other oonstitueney EIS to the intensity and extensive- ness of the disease from which it suffers. The Com- missioners' report shows ,that they have reason to believe that there never was a contested election fought in Macclesfield on really pure principles, and the disclosures made clearly demonstrate that under the present law regarding the conduct of Parliamen- tary election it would be hopeless to expect that there ever will be one. The whole place appears to be saturated with electoral iniquity, for it would seem that bribery has become so common there, and the voters are so used to it, that they apparently believe they cannot do without it. The Parliamentary register of Macclesfield contains 6,962 names, and the Cemmissioners schedule no less than 2,872 persons as having been guilty of corrupt practices of some kind or another. So even supposing all who engaged in . 'violating the law at the last election have been found out, nearly one-half of the entire constituency is corrupt. Probably the Commiesioners experienced a feeling of surprise and gladness to learn that there was even. one politically righteous voter in the place. We questinn, however, whether the whole story .is yet told, for although it is very unlikely that the Commissioners would schedule any one who did not deserve it, it is more than probable that there are many names absent which have as much right as any to be there. The evidence adduced before the Corn- misieners clearly showed that open and undisguised treating distinguished the elections of 1865, 1868, and 1874, and that on these occasions the Liberals ' outshone the Conservatives in illegal liberality. At , the 1880 election, however, there seems to have been a I sort of duel of corruption, in which the two parties had agreed on the choice of a weapon, and had it fairly measured previous to combat. A fund of £2,000 was raised by the Liberals for the purpose of instilling political principles into the minds of the electors, and the Conservatives did the same thing. After this preliminary the fight went on in earnest, and no one whose rectitude was not immovable was left una'ssailed by the voice of the tempter, The most familiar method adopted was the employment of voters as paid canvassers. The Conservatives had the .biggest success in this, 'for—although the employment of one such canvasser is sufficient to jeopardise a seat —they had no less than nine hundred and fifty on their botdrs, whilst the Liberals had eight hundred and seventy. One witness told the Commissioners that the Liberals had resolved to fight the Conservatives with • their own weapons and this appears to have been the spirit of the Conservatives, but how the necessity for { this arose we fail to see as the weapons in each case appears to have always been the same—well-filled money bags. The Commissioners found that 4,000 out of the total EX:2 voters on the register were mid in one way or another, and one of the most disgrace- ful features of the last election there was the preva- lence of corruption in high places /or it included councillors, aldermen, and even justices of the peace. Here were men set in authority in the town and who should have been examples as law,abiding citizens who openly and unblushingly broke the law and tram- pled it under their feet. Such a scandalous state of things should be put an end to by means of strong measures. A.c' long as we treat bribery and corrup- tion with a degree of tenderness and consideration which would be considered highly objectionable in other illegal practices, we must be prepared to find an amount of levity and indifference regarding it which bodes no good to the electoral character of a con- stituency. We are glad, therefore, to learn that the Government have resolved to take action iri these cases. We learn that Mr. John May and Mr. Wm. Mair, the Liberal and Conservative agents at the last election, who were reperted by the Commissioners as guilty of bribery and 'corruption and furnishing untrue ac- counts, have received an intimation from the Attorney- General that he intends to :institute prosecutions against them. This is a step do the right direction. It would have been the subject of unfavourable corn- ment—and ,rightly so too—if the illiterate and not over scrupulous sellers of their electoralprivikges had been prosecuted, while those who had fonnd the money for the purchase had been allowed to go scot free.

A very amusing instance of a countryman's idea of the Utility of the new registered envelope' supplied by the postal authorities occurred the other day. The gentleman I refer to, having occasion to send away £2O, invested in one of these new envelopes, in order to ensure the money reach- ing its destination safely. He then placed 20 Sovereigns within the envelope, and, enclosing it in a larger one, addresesd it to the firm he wished to remit to, and carefully deposited it in the letter box, feeling perfectly satisfied that he had done a wise and prudent action. Tenpence had to be paid upon delivery for extra registration fees and postage; and upon being communicated with, 'my friend stated that he imagined that the security afforded by the registered envelope lay in its peculiar construction, being evidently of opinion that it was a sort of portable thief-proof safe !

I do not think that the Rev. S. F. Green has any reason to envy the Irish prisoners in Kilmainham Gaol the luxuries they enjoy, during their experience of durance vile. Mr. Green, like the other Ritualistic clergy who have been im- prisoned for not obeying the powers that be, is, of course, in the happy position of a first-class misdemeanant, and not subject to strict prison discipline. His room has been car- peted by his congregation, and some of the young ladies have taken him a choice bouquet, and he is able to draw upon the cuisine of a neighbouring hotel for the require- ments of the inner ,nan. I dare say, we shall be told that he is another "martyr for conscience sake." If so, I fancy some of my readers will be inclined to say that it is fairly comfortable martyrdom.

A very amusin-tr and singular incident occurred the other evening which should be a warning to all young people who practice strolling near the canal. A youiAg Kentlemsn and his "dearly beloved," whilst walking on the banks of the canal, were so intent upon building castles ha the air that they omitted to notice how near they were going to the edge of the bank. Suddenly their "soft whisperings" were rudely stopped, in consequence of the lady missing her foot- ing, and as her lover's arm was round her waist, both of them were precipitated into the water. Fortunately their cries for help were heard by two workmen, who rescued the hap- less couple from what might have proved a watery grave, as neither of them could swim. On being brought safe to terra _firma, the amorous swain was profuse in his expres- sions of gratitude to his rescuers, the value he placed upon his own and his darling's life being shown by a present to th; two workmen of sixpence, to be divided between them! One of the men very coarsely remarked that " if the job was not worth more than that it was worth nothing at all," and he refused to accept any portion of the handsome (2) gift. Whether tbe young lady agreed with the workman I cannot say, but I am strongly inclined to do so, and I would remind the fair damsel that she now knows her value in her lover's eyes.

A lady has written to me to say that when walking through the streets out of every hundred men she met on the footp ith an average of three turned out for her. The others invariably kept right on towards her, leaving her to go to the right or left of them as she chose. She wishes to know whether this disposition of men and women not to. yield an inch of walk, especially where an old lady or an old man must get out of the way, is due to stupid ignorance or selfishness. I give it up. The weather we have lately experienced certainly excuses the jocosity of the foreigner in his description of our climate. A Yankee once said that in England there was no climate it was all weather. I presume that Dr. Laird Collier never heard of that, else he would never have come to live in England far the sake of its climate. This is what the doctor has done, and the act shows courage and confidence of a phenwinenal kind. Most, if not all, of my readers will agree with me that ours a seductive climate. Its sudden transitions from genial sunny weather to told east winds and heavy snowstorms ought to be enough of themselves to lure the traveller hither. Our BUlTlmers have lately been so dry and our winters so mild, our atmosphere so bracing and skies so clear, that the only wonder is that our enterprising Yankee cousins don't start a company for moving the United States and anchoring them alongside England. No doubt, when Dr. Laird Collier reports to them what at charming climate we have, we may expect,a great immigra• tion of American iprvalids, 19r they will scarcely believe the remarks of the Frenchmau who, having been used to bright blue -skies and sunny atmosphere, said that in England there were eight months of wicter and aitir months of bad weather.

SNG .4F THE STATIONS OF TEE CROSS.—A tolerably fine morning having succeeded to the rather unpleasant weather lof the previous-days, many persons took advantage of the favourable change to repair to St. Michael's, Ditton, to wit- ness the solemnities that had beea previously .announced to takeplace there last Sunday. When high mass began at 1040 a.m. the church was well filled, and those who had xot been there since the previous Sunday must _have been agreeably surprised at the new and pleasant aspect given to , the aisles by the fourteen large and beautiful paintings that ' imparted (life and animation to their previouslv naked walls. , Mass was celebrated by the Rev. F. Bienen, of Fortino., assisted IT the Rev. G. Locher, as master of ceremonies. The music of the mass was the composition of De Witt, a distinguished composer of the day in )G-ermany. The choir, under the able direction of the -Rev. C. Recite, acquittedi itself with that marked ability which kas distinguised it on every occasion, while the Rev. Mr. Evers was still true to himself at the organ. After the gospel, the Rev. F. De Hasa lascended the pulpit, and taking for his text the wards of St. John, "And hearing his own moss he went forth to that place.called Calvary," delivered a discourse appropriate to , the occasion. The attendance at the afternoon service WAS even larger than it had been in the mornigg. The nave and 'both the ailes were completely filled. The service began by the priest intoning at the steps of the altar the Veal Creator, which was taken up and eeng through by the choir, the priest proceeding meanwhile with the ceremony of the blessfng of the crosses that were to be placed on the; several stations. A procession was .next fermed, and pro-f ceeded from the sanctuary to the first station, before which, after one of the crosses had keen placed upon it, a short meditation en the scene in the Passion it represented WAS read aloud, followed by an appropriate prayer. The proems-, sion then moved on to the second station, the choir singing a verse of the " Stabat Mater," by Nanini. In this manner, the entire way of the cross was made, the whole congrega- tion tureing in the direction of each station as the proces- sion moved towards it. The ceremony was simple and beautiful, and its effect on the congregation was visible in the marked attention and devotion with which they fellowed the priest from station to station throughout the whole cere- mony. When the procession had re-entered the sanctuary, the hymn of thanksgiving, the Te Deum, was recited. The altar was then prepared for solemn benediction, and in the interval the children sang the beautiful hymn. "0, Jesus,. Jesus, dearest Lord," with such taste and precision as re- flected no little •credit on the careful training they bad received from the Rev. F. Guggenberger. After the bene- diction the Rev. Father de Haza again addressed the con- gregation on the fruits of the devotion of the way of the cross—Vote,

_ Now ESCAPE OP Mu. fficictistsON, HMlTlcros TO THE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.--On Saturday evening, Mr. Thomas Higginson, of Widnes, who is surveyor to the Local Beard, was a passenger from Broadheath to Widnes, by the train due at the latter station at 6-15. On its arrival, he alighted whilst the carriages were in motion and fell between the footboards on to the line, so that his body was between the line and the platform. Mr. Sansom, the station master, who was standing within a few yards of the spot, saw that the wheels of the carriages were just clearing Mr. Higgin• son, and shouted to him in stentorian tones "Don't move." For a few seconds the utmost excitement prevailed amongst the numerous passengers, and some of the ladies screamed so loudly as to be heard in Victoria-road, Two or three carriages passed Mr. Iligginson before the train could be brought to a standstill, after which lie was helped on to the platform, and found to have enaped injury. This is some- what miraculous, is there 'are only about 18 inches between the line and the kerb.

THE FOOT AND MOUTH Drsaaan.—On Wednesday information was received from the Clerk of the Peace at Preston that six places recently declared infected by foot and mouth disease were now free from contagion, and it is stated that the epidemic is fast dying out. MANsLantinTER AT WlGAN.—Daniel O'Neil was remanded by the Wigan magistrates, on Monday, on a charge of having caused the death of John Leary, an over- looker at a cotton mill. It seems that the wives of the men quarrelled on Sunday, when Leary came up with the object of separating them. 0 Neil objected, and struck Leary in the face, breaking the bridge of his nose and knocking him to the ground. Leary fell on an old grid close to his own doorstep, and was picked ttp insensible. He died on Mon- day morning.

MERSEY' SALT AND BRUNS COMPANY, Maur company is formed with a capital of £250,000 in shares of £lO each, to raise brine from the great salt deposits on the estate of A. H. Smith-Barry, Esq., of Marbury, Cheshire, conveying it in iron pipes to Runcorn, and erecting there extensive works capable of producing 200,000 tons of salt per annum, by which means it can be manufactured at a cost considerably less than at existing works in in the salt districts. The arrangements will include the supply of brine in its natural state to the chemical manufacturers of Run- corn, and a subsequent extension to Widnes and St. Helens is also contemplated. By the acquirement of a valuable agreement and various concessions detailed in the prospectus Published in our advertising columns, the company antici- pate effecting a saving of 20 per cent. on all salt manufac- tured at Runcorn as well as a saving in the cost of coal so that it is expected that a profit en the manufacture at that port alone will give a dividend of 20 per cent., whilst a farther source of profit is anticipated from the supply of brine in its natural state to chemical manufacturers of the district.

DRAMATIC ENTERTAINMENT, WINSFORD.—The Amateur Dramatjc Society, at NVinsford, gave their final entertain- ment for the season in the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Previously invitations have been issued, but this time it was open to the public, and as the hall was very full no doubt the proceeds would be satisfactory. The entertainment con- sisted of a short concert succeeded by a dramatic perfor- mance, after which a dance was kept up for some hours with great enjoyment to its participators. The performance fully' kept up the character the society has obtained.

WINSFORD IMPRovntEms.—The activity of the mem- bers of the Local Board in devising and carrying out im- provements in this town, at such a rate as not to be too heavy on the rates, is now manifested in the direction of Weaver-street. The lowering of the street by the removal of a lot of rubbish which will give way to macadam, will be a real improvement carried out not a minute too soon. The changes which have occurred within the last five years are not few or inexpensive, but the rates have risen propor- tionately.

EXCITING SCENE IT A CHAPEL.—On Sunday, shortly before twelve o'clock, there occurred a most exciting scene at Pole-street Baptist Chapel, Preston. The new minister, the Rev. M. Goodchild, frem Mr. Spurgeon's Tabernacle, was preaching, when an alarm of fire was raised, and it was found that a portion of the gallery was blazing, having been set on fire by the over-heating of the flues. The congrega• tion ran precipitately into the street. Fortunately there were some cool beads amongst those present, and no one was injured. The fire brigade was sent for, and soon extin- guished the flames. ELEINGTON ELSE:EXTANT SCHOOLS. The report of the schools of William Bashall and Co., (Messrs. McMinnies) appears to be remarkably good this year. The inspector says—Mixed school.—" The whole of the elementary work is done with' very great accuracy, the failures being ex- tremely few and many of the slates and papers quite fault- less. Handwriting is excellent. Besides this, both the read- ing and class subjects shew great intelligence and power of answering readily. Singing is particularly good and sewing has been very carefully taught." Infants school.—" The Wants have been taught with very great care and passed an excellent examination. They are also in very good order." The head master of these schools is Mr. R. Paine, formerly of this town.

PRESENTATION AT WYCLIFFE SCHOOL, WARRINOTON.— In presentation WAS made on Monday evening, in the Wycliffe School, to Miss Jessie Rutherford, who is about to leave Wartington for Australia. The presentation was preceded by a tea, which was laid out in the class- room, and to which about 30 people sat down. After tea, Mr. Blackwood, the superintendent of the school, said they had met that night to perform an act which was both pleasing and painful—pleasing because they were about to testify to one of their number their affection and esteem for her and painful because she was about to leave them for a dis- tant land. From what he knew of Miss Rutherford he believed her to be worthy of this mark of their esteem. She WAS going to a tar-off shore, but he hoped that when there she would not forget the friends she had left behind. Mr. Beswiek endorsed Mr. Blackwood's remarks as to the pre- sentation being made with mingled feelings of joy and re- gret, and said Miss Rutherford had for some time been a member of his class, and he thought they had all every reason to respect her. After some further remarks, M. Beswick made the presentation, which consisted of a case ef handsome books and an illuminated card, on which were set forth the particulars of the presentation. Mr. Frank Ruther- ford, on behalf of his sister, acknowledged the presentation. BISHOP FEARER AND THZ PRESENT CRISIS IN THE Cauncw.—On Tuesday, at the Diocesan Registry, a memo- rial hearing the signatures of 355 clergymen was presented to the Bishop of Manchester, with respect to certain changes which it was considered desirable should be made in the constitution of the Church with regard to its legislative and judicial functions. The memorial was presented by the Archdeacon of Manchester, in presence of a number of the local clergy. The Bishop, in his reply, said that he did not find anything in the memorial sufficiently definite to guide his own course ieither in Parliament or in the administration of his diocese. As to the constitution of the Court of Final Appeal he was at issue with the memorialists in the sugges- tion which they made, and expressed his belief that to con- stitute such 'court on a bass calculated to secure general approval" was an utter impossibility. He announced his intention of moving a resolution in the Convocation of York to the effect that the rubric which had been the cause, from its ambigcity, of all their differences and disaster ought to be removed, and a new and intelligible rubric free from am- biguity put in its place. That, he thought, was the only solution of the difficulty. His earnest desire was to see pease aid unity restored to the distracted Church of Eng- land, but unless men would abandon some of their wilful- ness he knew not hew this was to be attained.

A. Beet, and that in the•evening by the superintendent minister. the Rev. E. 0. Coleman. The services were attended by large congrega- tions, and the collections realised £lO ss. 10d. CHILD FOUNRI DEAD THE CANAL, IT SANKEY BRIDOES.—Mr. T. W. Barker, the deputy coroner, held an In-Attest at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, on Wednes day afternoon, touching the death of a newly-born male rchild, which had been found in the canal at about 11 .o'clock on Tuesday morning, by, Martin Towle, a horse • driver. Mr. T.Starkey Smith, who had made a post ',torten* -examination crT the body, said there were 'no external marks of violence, not was there any fracture of the skull. The lungs were partially inflated, and both sides of the heart were full of blood, showing that the child had lived. Death had been caused either by want of attention at birth or by suffocation, but whether by drowning or external pressure he could not-say. The child had been born from ten days to a fortnight.—The jury returned ausspen verdict. Messrs. J. Andrews, A. Andrews, Arthur Bennett, -J. Wilde, and W. J. Bennett agreed with the essayist's views, whilst Messrs. PRINCE OF. WALES THEATRE, WARRINGTON. —The theatre during the week has been occupied by a company, under the management at Mr. Richard Edgar, and organised by Mr. J. L. Toole, for the performance olMr. Henry J. 13yron's comedy, "The Upper Crust." The piece is replete with rich humour and vivacious wit, combined with many absurd situations, a remarkably good impromptu concluding Gle second act. The construction of the comedy, and the excellent manner in which each character is sustained by the various members of the company, does not allow the interest to flag for an instant, the audience being convulsed with laughter almost the whole of the evening. To-night is the last eight en which it will be performed in War- rington.

WARRINGTON UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE Com- atirrEE.—The monthly meeting of this committee was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday. Mr. R. Garnett presided. and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Rev. J. Tongs, Messrs. J. Marsh, P. Hall, S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and B. Hodson (attendance officer). Mr. Hobson reported an increase in each school average on the list. In the detailed weekly list the committee would find that he had shown four weeks which he had compared with five weeks in the previous list, and the four weeks beat the five weeks in having a larger average attendance. He had visited several schools in the district, and found that now the attendance was improving regularly. He was glad to learn that the bye-laws had been returned as finally approved. The committee had now done with the costly school attendance orders, except in very bad cases. If they wished to get an order of commit- ment to a certified industrial school, the committee then ap- plied in the first instance for a school attendance order. He submitted to be proceeded against 10 cases of parents who i had neglected to send their children to school. The health of the district among the children was better than last I month, and he hoped that the fever would be stamped out , very soon. The attendance officer was instructed to take proceedings against Lawrence Sachill, Tbelwall ; John Muskett, Latchford; James Ditchfield and George Howarth, ; Martinscreft ; Peter Eythgoe, Fearnhead; John Rowles, Joseph lligham, and Enoch Hewitt, Houghton Green. The lbye-laws stated that the parent of every child of not less ' than 5 nor more than 13 years of age should cause such 1 child to attend school, unless there be a reason- able excuse for non-attendance. But it was provided that a child between ten and thirteen years of age should not be reonired to attend to school if such child had received a cer- tificate that it had reached the fifth standard, and that a child between ten and thirteen years of age could be em- ployed" half time" if such child had received a certificate that it had reached the fourth standard. Every parent who did not observe the bye-laws, or any of them, would on con- viction be liable to a penalty not exceeding, with costs ss. for each offence. The averages for the four weeks ending March 19th were :—Orford 157, increase 43 ; Penketh 127, increase 27; Winwick 93, increase 23; Grappenhall. 85, increase 10; Hollinfare 94, increase 8; Martinscroft 77, increase 21; Padgate 85, increase 17; Thelwall 74, increase 17; Sankey 84, increase 18. This being the last meeting of I the committee for the year, the Rev. J. Yonge proposed, and Mr. Hall seconded, a vote of thanks to the chairman and vice-chairman for their services during the year, and the chairman having replied, the meeting terminated.

THE TRawsvear,.—Eal KIMBERLEY, replying to Lord Carrington, said that a British Force of 12,000 men was now in South Africa. In reply to Lord Brabourne, Earl Kimberley quoted a memorandum from the President of the Transvaal Republic to show that there was no general system of slavery in the Transvaal. The Government had no in- formation of the attack on Pretoria. The Local Courts of Bankruptcy (Ireland) Bill passed through committee, and the House adjourned.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. A MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. Sir M. LOPES gave notice to move a resolution in favour of the appointment of a Minister of Agriculture. AFGHANISTAN.— Lord HARTLNGTON, replying to Mr. O'Donnell, said Ayoob Khan was not in prison, but undtt surveillance. It is not the intention of the Government to assist the return of Ayoob Khan to Afghanistan, or take any steps that might increase anarchy in the country. SOUTH AFRICA.—Mr. CHILD said they were not with- drawing troops from South Africa. They had intercepted three regiments and one battery proceeding there. There were at present 12,000 men in the South African command. THE PROSECITTION OF A NEWSPAPER EDITOR. The ArromEY-Gmanar, said the editor of the Freiheit was arrested on a warrant issued on sworn information that he had committed a statutable offence. The premises were locked up to protect the property.

. . . Din TRANSVAAL. Mr. CHILDERS said there was no truth in the rumour that certain regimeats had been sent to the Transvaal owing to the incompetency of the commanding officers. Mr. GRANT DLTFF said they had had a telegram that day from Sir E. Wood, and as no mention was made of a sortie from the British garrison having been repulsed by the Boers inflicting great loss, he believed the report published was inaccurate.—Mr. CHILDERS promised to telegraph to the Cape for information on the subject.—Mr. GLADSTONE would lay on the table as much of the instructions as pos- sible to the Royal Commissioners at the Cape at the eat-lest moment. He could not produce the whole of them. A NEw WRIT.—A new writ was issued for St. Ives. THE REPRESENTATION OF NORTHAMPTON.—Mr. LABOII- CHERE moved the issue of a new writ for Northampton in the place of Mr. Bradlaugh, who sinee his election had vacated his seat in Parliament by sitting and voting in the House without having taken and subscribed the oath pre- scribed by law.—Sir R. CROSS said they ought to have the views of the Government before the writ was issued. He thought the writ ought not to be issued before the appeal was decided by the House of Lords.—Mr. LABOUCHERE said Mr. Bradlaugh accepted the decision as to not having the right to sit. The appeal to the House of Lords was on the point of right of a common informer to sue. He depre- cated the raising of another Bradlaugh debate.—The ATTORNEY•GENERAL said the point raised for the House of Lords would be simply on the right to sue for the penalty. As Mr Bradlaugh accepted the decision adverse to his retaining his seat, he thought it would be but just:ce to the electors of Northampton that the writ should be issued.—Mr. GORST expressed surprise at the course proposed by the Attorney General. He objected to the writ being issued.— After Mr. Morgan Lloyd, Mr. C Lewis, and Sergeant Simon had made some observations, Sir S. .NORTHCOTE said he would not oppose the issue of the writ, but he threw on the Government the responsibility of the position in which the House might find itself.—Mr. GLAD- STONE accepted the responsibility. He said neither he nor his colleagues had any communication with Mr. Bradlaugh beyond whether under the circumstances it would be conve- nient for him to apply for the Chiltern Hundreds. He defended the resolution that had been passed, and said the present result was its best justification.—The motion for issuing the writ was agreed to.—Sir HERBERT MAXWELL called attention to the effect of unrestricted importation of spurious compounds from America resembling butter. He moved a resolution stating the advisability of the Legisla- ture taking steps that would ensure as far as possible that such of those compounds as are harmless should only be sold under distinctive names, and that the import,ttion and sale of those which were hurtful and dangerous to teeth be prohibited altogether. Mr. ARTHUR MOORE thought it absolutely necessary for the protection of the poor that steps should be at once adopted to prevent butterine beitold as butter, and thereby prevent working people being robbed of their money by. spurious commodities being imposed on them as the genuine article.—Mr. A. ARNOLD thought the Adulteration of Food Act should be so amended as to bring all articles of human food under its provisions.—Dr. PLAY- FAIR said the farmers must meet the competition, and if they failed to do so the result wonld be the chemist would beat them out of the market. He did not think oleomar- garine prejudicial to health, and considered it much to be preferred to bad and ill-made butter.—Viscount FOLKESTONE said the prohibition of importation was not required. All that was wanted by the farmer was that these scientific compounds should not be sold as butter.—Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN said it had been clearly proved that butterine was not prejudicial to health, and if it was prevented coming into this country, the poorer classes would be the sufferers.—Mr. PELL said that when he was in America he visited one of the places where this butterine was manufactured, and he found nothing objectionable to exist, but quite the contrary. He could not advise the prohibition of the importation of butterine into this country: Mr. Snew Insisted that butterine should be sold under its proper name. He did not believe good butter would over be beaten out of the market. LEFT SITTINELf

WIGAN ELECTION PETITION. MR. F. S. POWELL UNSEATED. After an hour's hearing, yesterday, upon a representation made by Mr. Mathews, the leading counsel for the respon- dent, Mr. F. S. Powell (the respondent) withdrew from any further defence. Mr. Mathews said he could not contend against the conclusive cases of bribery and agency that had been proved, but claimed exoneration for Mr. Powell and his solicitors, Messrs. Darlington, who had been censured by their lordships for obtaining statements from the Liberal witnesses during the course of the inquiry. Mr. Justice Grove said DO charge was made against Mr. Powell personally, and therefore no reply was needed. As regarded the other 1 gentlemen, who had been censured, his lordship could not say that the instructions of Mr. Matthews relieved those gentlemen from the blame which the court thought proper to impose upon them.—Mr. Mathews applied for costs, on the ground that the petitioners put forward were not proper representatives of the Liberal party.—Mr. Day, in reply, denounced in most emphatic terms the gross and wholesale corruption which had been disclosed, and expressed complete surprise at the application from a side which had not only been guilty of the grossest bribery, but some of the merabera of which had incurred the censure of the court by tampering with witnesses. The petition was that of the entire Liberal party, who desired to vindicate the political freedom of the constituency, and to free the town from this great scandal.—Mr. Ralph Darlington and Mr. John Appleton (Conservative solicitors) were (-tiled by Mr. Mathews to prove that although they had taken certain depositions they had not in any way attempted to influence the witnesses. The judges retired to consider these questions, and upon returning; Mr. Justice Grove, after a lengthy review of the , case, gave judgment that Mr. Powell must be uuseated in consequence of the acts of his agent, Mr. Thomas Scott, the general secretary. The instances in which voters were brought from Whiston and paid 10s. each at the office of the Conservative Association were quite conclusive, as was the circular issued by Mr. Nathaniel Eckersley and Mr. Scott u to agency. The judges would be bound to report to the Speaker of the House of Commons that there was reason to believe that corruption existed in the borough to a large ex- tent. The court ordered Mr. Powell to pay all his own costs, and also £2,000 towards the costs of the petitioners. His lordship commented in terms of surprise and indigna- tion at the condition of some ef the witnesses, who appeared to regard it a duty honourable to them to accept a bribe. EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF THE SULTAN. A Central News telegram from Paris to-day says r-11 auk informed on the highest authority that the Sultan has pro- posed to the French Government to depose the Khedive and replace him by anyone the French Government may select. This was intended to destroy England's influence in Egypt. I further learn that the French Government peremptorily rejected the proposition, and informed the English Govern- ment of the Sultan's communication. The affair has caused great excitement among diplomatists here. APPOINTMENTS BY HER MAJESTY. Her Majesty has been pleased to appoint General Sir W. Fenwick Williams, Bart., to the vacant office of Constable of the Tower. The Queen has also been pleased to approve of the appointment of Sir R. Matins as member of the Privy Council. INCREASE OF MINERS' WAGES IN THE MAN- CHESTER DISTRICT. It has been decided by some of the leading colliery firms in the Manchester district to give their underground em- ployes an advance of wages at the beginuing of next week. This is, we believe, in accordance with the intirhation which was given to the men before the recent strike in this district, that if the prices of coal were maintained the ques- Lion of wages would be favourably considered.

. - REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OP COAL. A redaction in the price of coal has been announced by the Earl of Dudley. Coal is down Is . and slack 6d. per ton. This leaves west of Dudley best household 125., and east of Dudley thick furnace coal 95., forge and steam is., and engine slack 4s. Bd. per ton. The alteration carries a re- duction of 3d. and lid. per day respectively in Staffordshire colliers' wages. It will be followed by a drop of 10s. per ton in some sorts of finished iron. THE TRANSVAAL. News which if true toay have serious consequences reaches us from Nital. It is stated, on dubious authoriiy, that the British garrison at Pretoria recently made a sortie against the Boers, and were driven back with much loss. The Bosra who communicated the information had brought despatches from Pretoria for Mr. Kruger. They. stated that the Boers who have been set free by the surrender of Potchefstroom had joined the besiegers of Pretoria, and aided them in re- pulsing the sortie. It will be seen that the attack was made by the British, and it is incredible, supposing the affair took place during the armistice, that Sir Owen Lanycn was aware that a suspension of heatilities had been agreed upon. It follows, therefore, that General Joubert bad not fulfilled btia promise to inform the various British garrisons of the I armistice.

The Greek Government and the newspapers are represented' as being strongly opposed to the acceptance of the new line proposed by Turkey. The only answer to the despatch from Constantinople has been, it is said, increased activity in the War Depaitment. LORD BEACONSFIELD'S HEALTH. Lord Beaconsfield has been suffering from a severe attack of bronchial asthma associated with undeveloped gout, and much anxiety has been manifested for him during the last fen days. The latest bulletin, issued at 9-45 on Thursday night, is as follow:—" Lord Beaconsfield has passed a quitt day, and his lordship's symptoms to-night are rather more favourable."

div.head: PROSECUTION OF A NEWSPAPER EDITOR.
div.p: PROSECUTION OF A NEWSPAPER EDITOR.

Johann Most was charged at Bow-street Police Conr',,, ti Thursday, with having published in the Fr!iheit 's scan- dalous, wicked, and malicious libel concerning the )ate Czar, and with encouraging divers persona to Y.ommit the crime of murder. The particular article was read commenting on the Czar's death, in which the late Emperor is called a "monster," and "one of the most horrible tyrants of Europe." "Th. ter- rible news, says the article, " rang like a thunderclap in the princely castles wherein dwell the guilt-laden ones who have a thousand times over merited a like fate. Long for- feited heads tremble from Constantinople to Washington. Could only one such crowned ragamuffin be destroyed per month, there wouldCbe slight desire to play at monarchy." Evidence was given of the seizure of materials at the print- ing office. I'risoner, who admitted being the editor of the paper, was remanded fer a week, bail being refused.

I quired to heat the water in a small cylinder ' starting all ' cold, is about 2to ours with a burner consuming 10 cubic feet of gas per hour and this quantity of gas can be safely burnt in any small bathroom with both door and window closely shut. In the absence of special flues it is the only system possible with gas, without danger. If hot water is wanted continuously, a very tiny flame, kept in, will do all necessary when the water is once hot To use gas in a small close bath-room at the rate of 70 to 100 cubic feet per hour is equivalent to putting a large char- coal brazier in the room, either would cause suffocation in a 1 few minutes. We have used gas for many years, to the total exclusion of fires, for cooking water heating, and daily baths. Our family consists of 10 persons, and our average daily gas consumption from all cooking and water heating purposes does not exceed 40 feet per day, average cost 1d: Our total consumption for lighting is on an average 150 cubic feet per day, cost 6d., and we burn in one room, every evening, more gas for lighting only than is used all over the house for cooking, baths, and all work of this class. It is, therefore, absurd to say that the quantity of gas need , for cooking can be either injurious or dangerous. Abad cook- ing burner and also a tad lighting burner will make itself disagreeable by the formation of a trace of acetyline and carbonic oxide. The remedy is simple: see that the burn-r in fault is made right or replaced. Gas has been used too long for lighting purposes to admit of any foolish state- ments being allowed to pass without question," and ventila- tion is rarely thought of in ordinary dwellings. It is also evident that for cooking gas is absrolutely safe even when used freely, and when the fact is once clearly understood that when burnt in large quantities for heating water rapidly it requires a free and direct exit for the products of combus- tion, the present scare will disappear and accidents will be unknown. The Makers of high power water heaters are greatly to blame for not insisting on the tact that a special flue must ba provided. This necessity is well known to most, and its non-publication can only be accounted for by the knowledge that people would not buy instantaneous water heaters if they, as is the case in most bath-rooms, could not put in a satisfactory flue to take away the producta of combustion. THE RECENT TOWNSHIP MEETING AT . Sir,— In reading ever the report of the Weston township I meeting, I notice that Mr. Poole, one of the overseers, stated that the recent legal proceedings taken against Mr. VVillierri Bankes, for the recovery of his poor rate, were instituted On the advice of Mr. Henry Linaker, Prodsham. This was not se. The overseers did act upon legal advice, but not frem Mr. Henry Linaker.—Yours truly, ' JAMES COLLIER, Assistant Overseer.
