COMMUNISM IN ENGLAND. Sir —Prejudice is said to be the offspring of ignorance, and I must say that your correspondent "J." hiss gone far to verify that saying in his futile attack upon W.'ts " , letter in your issue of March 12th. " J.'s' letter from be- ginning to end is composed of a string of hackneyed phrases • that fall on the ear constantly, and which, as a rule, eta- . Bate from superficial brains, whose highest ideal of life con- sists in the worship of "investments," "money,' "capital," " property," &c. Lam not going to set myself the task ; , of defending "H. W.," as I feel fully convinced from his able letter that he can soon pierce the armour of this modern "Don Quixote." But there are two points I should like to notice in " Ps" letter, because of their utter falla- ciousness and the common misunderstanding that exists • upon those points. But, before I proceed to notice those two points, I would call " Vs" attention to his erroneous conception of "H. W.'s" idea, anent the distribution of land amongst the people as private property,. I have read and se-read "H. W.'s" letter, and fail to find one sentence that advocates the distribution of land amongst the people as private property. What "H. W." advocates is nationalize- 'than of land not distribution ; and distinctly recommends the public purchase of land from present proprietors at a fair price. And "J." can't object to that, because the prin- ciple has already been applied in the case of railways and public buildings. The first important point I propose deal- ing with as being tenacious and misleading is as follows: —" We have not yet in England 'descended to the depths of Communised." But what is Communism? Ah ! there's the rub ; and "3." has left us in the dark as to the peculiar and repulsive aspects in which it appears to his mind. Only _ this is clear, viz., it is a descent from some lofty ideal exist- ing in the imagination of "J." Now, without going back into the history of England, OA let us take a glance at the tendencies of Englishmen in a few of the various departments of our soeial and political life. Taking the ordinary family as a starting point, what do we see but an almost pure communism during. -the early period of its existence? Surely "J." is not blind to that important fact. Or is "J." some disappointed old bachelor, left an orphan in early life, and so has not tasted' the sweets of connnunism as enjoyed in a happy English family? Take the army and navy in their social and domestic arrangements; is there no communism there? Has "3." ever been to Oxford or Cambridge and visited those splendid balls and colleges of learning, and not dis- covered a "descent into the depths of communism ?" What are our religious organisations if not communistic in their , fundamental principles? Amidst all their theological differences, have they not a common object in view? Nay, do they not preach and teach concerning a communistic heaven, and--. But I shall be told those places are not in England. What of all our philanthropic institutions, our sick and burial societies? Is communism ignored in any one - of them? In what light does "3." regavd our post-office, telegraphs, and public parks? Also our gigantic travelling arrangements by land and by sea? Surely "J " must have been living like the mole all his life, and invested himself as well as his money in his land, not to have realised the spirit of communism pervading this England of ours from John-o'-Groats to Land's End. Again I ask, for what pur- pose have we called into existence our local boards, munici- pal corporations, and our imperial Parliament, if we have not considered the common weal before aught else? Last, I and not least, what is the Underlying principle of all our • industrial co-operative organisations, whether for the sale or manufacture of the various articles of consumption that are required by its members? Perhaps "J." is not a member of the co-operative stores, and has never read a line of the • Co-operative News ;if so, he will not be able to follow me in the co-operative question. Yet if be will look at that 10 beautiful structure in Sankey-street, the Co-operative tr gore, and reflect that that has been built by common e . (or communistic) influences having been brought a to bear upon the minds of a goodly number - of the working men and women of Warrington; he will be compelled to acknowledge that, at least, in this par- ticular "we have in England descended to the depths of Communism." And what has been done in the matter of " stores can be accomplished with the land; in fact, if lam rightly informed, the Agricultural Labourers' Union, under the guidance of Mr. Joseph Arch, has to some extent ac- quired laael in their co-operative, ergo Communistic, capacity. •„.- So that, after all that can be said on this question of Coin- , munism, it is only a question of degrees in Communism. In this age we have been content to stop at Communistic shop- keeping and manufacture in a greater or leas degree. But a' who shall say how long we shall be content to remain at this stage of Communism? I have before me at this moment • a circular, drawn up by a solicitor, inviting the attention of all those whom it may concern to organise co-operative , colonies on various estates that are now in th 3 market. In . fact the walls of our borosigh are placarded by that same gentleman, inviting The attention of workingmen to the im- portance of colonising their own country, and not to emi- grate; and doubtless our children, who will be wiser than 1J" ourselves, will avail themselves of such opportunities astnay so be presented in their day to take back to themselves their • birthright, their inheritance—the land. "J." has evidently not vet learnt the first principles of the, relation that •sub- sists between the land and the people, and, until he has learnt his A B C, it is not to Se expected that he can understand the higher -lessons which a " descent " into " Communism ' is capable of teaching him. I b. cannot pass by a third point in "J.'s" letter without exposing the fallacy, viz, "Land simpl3! repre- sents money, or capital, like any other kind of , v.;• property." I should like to know what school of political ' t.,t, economy "J." has been educated in to utter such a fallacy •a" as that. It reminds me of looking at a mirror, before which was placed a raw of numerals, thus 1,2, 3,4, in the mirror they appear 4,3, 2,1. Now that is just what" J." has done.• ; He might as well have said that the master represents his servant; and if "J." cannot accept the doctrine, let him take ; , his pile of money into the heart of an uncivilised country 1 or desert and see what becomes of his representative pro- I o perty., Money mast perforce be' a servant, a representative, ' an invention of mile to do away with simple barter, hence it is a medium of exchange, a measure of price. Before "J." i; rushes into print again, to give utterance to such crude notions as he has done, I will advise him as be has advised W." "to study the subject a little more," and to rest am,:red that "there are more things in this world than are 41.?..ary,t of in his philosophy."--Yours, ac., LYNX.

WARRINGTON CORPORATION BATHS. Sir,—l was pleased to see in your last issue some very conclusive remarks on the prohibitory prices charged for the use of the public baths by the Corporation. I would ask for whose benefit were they erected if not for the working- man's ? And yet the charges are such as to be entirely be- yond his means. Those people whose incomes would allow them to use the baths do not require them, as they can in- variably aftOrd to have one fixed in their dwelling, which is ready for use at any time. But the workingman can afford no such luxury, and he is compelled, if he wishes to keep himself clean, to pay either is. or 6d. for a private bath. It is absolutely necessary for health, that a man who is employed in iron, glass, or chemical works, amid the grimy dust and vitiated atmosphere, and in any other trade, should frequently have a bathe, but the Corporation by their excessive charges preclude any possibility of this, and the heath of the town suffers in consequence. Surely the Corporation did not purchase the baths thinking to make them a source of revenue, for in few towns are they paying con- cerns. But even if they did, the case cited by you, Mr. Editor, shows that that object will be the best attained by low and reasonable charges, besides giving, what is of more importance, workingmen an opportunity of using them, and the Corporation if they are wise, and study the wants of the burgesses at large, will at once reduce their scale of charges, not only for the private baths, but for all.—Yours, HEALTH. ----- THE CASE OF MR. • . DEATH IN THE GAS. Sir,—Death after death and repeatednarrow escapes is con- nection with the use of a certain class of bath heaters, have , created a scare and terror which has extended to a fear of i the use of gas for any purpose. This fear has bees increased ' by certain foolish persoi 9 writing letters to the plthlic press, containing statements which have so grounds except in their own imaginations and which create serious mischief, and annoyance. As a matter of public duty it is time this state of things was settled, and put in such a form as to be easily understood, and the danger when it exists, read," says that the ily recognised. I One correspondent who signs himself " MD immense quantity of gas used for cooking is dangerous. With ' all due respect to "SI.D " this t • a' nplv nonsense; ~ statement Is tt . he evidently has no correct knowledge or information on the , 1 actual gas consumption in an average household for all pu matter. The tables which I enclose give day by day the poses. The name and position of the authority for these , figures are quite sufficient to vouch for their correctness, In 1 these it ifi shown that the daily consumption of gas for light- ing purposes is 113 cubic feet, the average daily consutnp- tion for cooking is 25 cubic feet. It is therefore evident that the danger, if it could exist, cannot be from the quantity of gas consumed for cooking, which for the whole day is less than what is burnt for lighting purposes in an ordinary Sit- ing room in one evening. The danger is here: it has become the fashion to expect to heat in perhaps 10 or 15 minute) a quantity of eater sufficient for a 20 or 30 gallon bath. It is well known that, of ali sub-
-------- tion, and why, or on what grounds ? If Mr. Shnffiebothain, or " LI. W." should write again let them endeavour to evolve, think out, and suggest some practical ideas.—l am, air,

yours truly, THE HOLIDAY SEASON AND CHEAP TRIPS. Sir,.-A5 the holiday season and fine weather is now ap- ProacilinZ, could not some of our large finns, such as Pilkington and Sons Cannington Shaw, and Co., Kurtz, and others, end ' endeavour to induce the railway com- panies to run cheap trains to Blackpool, Southport, dm., during the holidays, and to Liverpool every Saturday at say one and a quarter fare for the double journey (or return) so as to give their employes an opportunity of enjoying with their families the purer air of these seaside places, away from the smoke and smell of this town. I feel such a boon would be gratefully received, and would go far to cement a good feeling between the masters and their workpeople, which would tend to the advancement of each other's in- terest, and which should always exist between capital and labour r; for it is far better to dwell in harmony than in strife. I do hope this matter wlll be taken up by some more able pen than mine, and that the public at large will take an in- terest in the same. I feel assured that if the railway CCIIII.• pany be approached in a kindly manner, they will consider the case upon its merits, and no doubt concede the boon asked for. C. F. H. St. Helens, 30th March, 1881.

FROM THE CANON'S MOUTH. Sir,—l happened to be staying in Southport on Sunday a,nel Monday last, and taking up the Southport nsiter of Saturday, the 26th, I found the choice little blood and thunder Jingo poem, herewith enclosed. Its poetic merits are obvious. Its moral and Christian tone is sublime. But what is specially worthy of note is that the poem proceeds, as you may say, "from the canon's mouth," and hence no wonder that it is so warlike in its tone. It is, however, but very blank cartridge, and can do no harm unless it should help to explode the canon. Its author, who bides himself behind the initials" B. S. C." is a well known canon of the Established Church, famous in Conservative and Evangeli- cal circles in the good town of Southport. I send it you because it deserves as much notoriety as can be given to it, and because it shows to what length ministers of the Gospel of Peace can go when they once become votaries of the Earl of Beaconsfield.—Yours faithfully, A CONSTANT READER.

Warrington, March 28, 1881. "PEACE WITII DISTIONOUR.” When Beaconlield was warder, And watclid upon the tower, He brought " peace with honour And Britain felt her power. HC cheek'd the plots of Russia, Rept Germany in awe. And made the Rates of Europe Respect tt.e Lion's paw, The scientific frontier With foresight clear he plann'd, To guard our Indian Empire From foes on every head. But now his grasp is loosen'd: Another takes his place, And England's flag and acutcheon Are covered with disgrace. The wall we built in India— A menace to the Czar— We pull down with dishonour, And skulk from Candahar.

Can we be more degraded Yes, scandals stilt increase: The Boers leave beat the British; And now we sue for peace. Upon our necks, laid prostrate. Insulting foes have trod. Blot from our shield its tritruips— Write on it " Ichabod March 25th.
IL S. C.

CHESHIRE FARMERS' GRIEVANCES. Sir,—A hole and corner meeting took place lately in a village within sight of Helsby Hill, amongst the farmers under the rose, with the view of agitating for the three F's, viz.:—Fixity of Tenure, Fair Rents, and Free Sale. When I the question arose who should take the leading part and act as chairman, those well off and most independent began to make excuses; one said a good deal had been done for him, another that he expected to ;lave a field drained, a third ex- pected to have some more land added to his farm, a new house had been built for another to replace a dilapidated ode, a fifth hoped to be made under steward, and a sixth to get the post of chief butler and head bottle washer to Lord Tom Noddy with good pay and little to do. Those who had the largest holdings wanted the small ones to go to the front and bear the brunt lest on their names Teaching bead quar- ters, they might be served with a six months,notice to quit. Their courage gently oozed out at their fingers' ends, and they quietly sneaked away home, like sheep, dragging their tails behind them. Now I would strongly advise these valonrous farmers—who are airaid to call their souls their own—to enlist into the British Cavalry and offer their vain- able services to make short work of the Boers in the Trans- ' j vaal, where there would be an ample field and scope for the ' display of their pluck, bravery, and valour. AN OLD WOMAN.

A G freshov ernt discoveryent in one tbeei its made,coups. In such case they will of course bear no interest, and would be value- less as a Stock Exchange c)mraodity. Up to the present time 927 petitions, with 284,733 signa. tures, have been presented in favour of Mr. Bradlaugh's motion on perpetual pensions. Next week will be one of the busiest which even Mr. Gladstone has ever passed in his long public career. On Monday he is to introduce his Budget, and on Thursday he will explain the provisions of his Land Bill. Never in recent times has an English minister had two statements of such importance to make to the House of CoMmons. It is not surprising that Mr. Gladstone's friends look forward with 'some anxiety to a week of such labour; but I am glad to say that the right bon. gentleman is in excellent health, and there is every reason to believe he will be able, without undue strain, to perform the two tasks before him. The Rev. Dr. M'Cabe, Roman Catholic ArchbishcP of Dublin and Primate of all Ireland, is, it is stated, about to be created Papal legate in Ireland—an office to which no appointment has been made since the death. of Cardinal Cullen.

Great interest is felt in Wesley.ln circles just now res- pecting the next occupant uf the chair of the Conference From all I CAD hear the Rev. William Arthur, M.A., honorary secretary of the West ,yan Missionary Society, and President of the Wesleyan Conference when it was held in Leeds in 1866, is most likely to be elected to that important post. Mr. Arthur for years past has been eminent in the world of Methodism, and outside his own denomination is extensively known and universally beloved. His re-election to the presidential chair would be certain to give general satisfaction, for, in addition to his being one of the ablest of living Wesleyan ministers, he has bten one of the origi- nators of the forthcoming Methodist Cgcumenical Congress, and last year at Cincinnati represented the British Con- ference when the scheme was finally agreed upon. The only ground for fear is the precarious state of his health. He is now at Cannes, where he has spent the winter, an, I am Informed, is considerably better than he has been for some time past. In the event of Mr. Arthur not being physically equal, I understand that the coveted position will probably fall to the Rev. George Osborn, DR, Professor of Theology, Richmond College, who was president of the Conference in ISO, when it was held in Sheffield. It is arranged that the new president, whoever he may be, shall be the president of the Methodist (Ecumenical Congress, which is fixed to meet in London a month after the Wesleyan Conference has closed its sessions in Liverpool. Hence the strong desire in official circles to secure this year a minister, as president whose connexions' standing will at once command the sympathy and respect of Methodists of all shades through- out the world. I hear from a very good source that _further 'manipulation

- - of the Land. Bill in Cabinet Council has resulted in con- siderable concessionsto the views of those Ministers who desire to seize this grand opportunity of thoroughly settling the question. A great distaoce has been travelled since the Queen's Speech was brought in with the promise of a mea- sure to amend the Act of 1810. The process of conviction has been gradual, but it has been sure, and it will probably be found that the zest thing that could have happened both. to the Crovemment and to Ireland was the enforced delay, which has given opportunity for prolonged incubation of the measure. The Cabinet decision as described to me by a high authority is that the bill will go beyond the Duke of Richmond's report, will not go so far as Lord Bessborough's, strid will be moulded on the-lines of the minority report of the Radical section of the Royal Commission - The licensed victuallers are beginning to awake to the particular bearings of the Corrupt Fractices Lill upon the trade. Some of the classes are designed to bear very benvify upon publicans, making it penal to supply drink in particular circumstances. We shall hear a good deal of them when the bill comes on They are beginning to approach the Attorney-General on the subject of their grievances. The rusty pistol is unmaskad at last. After lying a week in charge of Inspector Denning at the House,. the mys- terious firearm was carefully removed by one of the detec- tive police, and taken down to Woolwich. This. morning the charge was extracted, and was found to consist of a packet of half-charred paper. The Home Secretary is in a considerable dithoulty with respect to the German Socialist paper, which is published in London, and recasionally shrieks aloud for the blood et monarchs. Its unseemly exultation over the assassination of the Caw has lifted it from its temporary obscurity, and the Home Secretary is ',now asked to put a stop to this publication. This can only be due by regulr.r process of law, andthe danger is felt that what is acluall7 insignifi- cant might by injudicious attention on the part of the authorities be mule famous. No representation on the subject has been made through the Foreign Office by Russit, but some oPthe Conservatives are urging the matter on the att-mtion of the Government, and will endeavour to goad them into action. Mr. Prior, of Manchester, the new assistant inspector of factories, has been appointed to the Birmingham dis-

trict. . Ureat interest is felt in voltintser circles concerning the proposed 14'iarch Irma London to the Sussex Downs for the Easter Monday review. Altogether it is anticipated that between 7,000 and 8,000 will take the road, part marching 'the entire distance, and others goings portion or toe way by train. Billeting accommodation has la en secured at Brigh- ton , for all the regiments that require it., The OA Strength of the various regiments of Lancashire Militia which are to be called tint for training this year is 10,522, which, added to the Volunteers; numbering 28,300, and the Yeomanry and Hussars, mating a total of nearly 40,000 for the auxiliary forces-of the County. Palatine. • Mr. Bradlaugh conducted his case on Wednesday with t marked ability. The junior. member for Northampton is not very successful as A speaker in the House of Commons. There he has too much of the manners of the platform; but he is highly successful in setting forth the results of 116. dustry and ingenuity after prolonged resenrch and note- taking in the library of the-House. The committee room is which the appeal was heard was at times very much crowded. • The tea merchants are in their annual condition of , flatter. Every March they get es mad- as a hatter, the- ex- citement Increasing as far into April as the Budget day may lie. In a less degree it is the same with the spirit merchants. Every man's trade lies so nearly home to himself that he I feels convinced that the Chancellor of the Exchequer must have his eye upon it to the exclusion of all else, and that it will figure largely in the forthcoming Budget. Apart from this natural tendency, the movement i 8 influenced by speculator!. All this is, however, founded upon conjecture. 'hem is at present nothing certain about the forthcoming Budget, except the statement you published some days ago that a peppy Will be taken off the income-tax, and that otherwise the tax will not be dealt with. This last is a contradiction of the positive statement that the Income-tax was to be materially reduced at the expense of the_succes- sion duty.
Inert- day k, Rector

right to close it. The Coroner suggested that the closing of the footpath would save many lives; and he went on further to say that he did not consider the case was one about which he need make any remarks. It was quite evidenc that, the two men who had been killed were going across the line at their own I risk, and with their lives in their hands. Their deaths had resulted owing to their oversight in not looking out for the second train. In reply to another remark from a jurymen, Mr. Ferrand said that if any of the gentlemen present could suggest a way of remedying the existing state of things, he had no deubt that the company would be very glad to take it up; but in order to prevent men going on to the line at such a place, a man would be needed at every ten yards of it. The Coroner : What you really want is for the company to have the management in Widnes instead of in London; but the public will not demand such a thing, and the con- sequence is that you will go on killing. The London and North-Western like to manage things up in the Metropolis, and the law allows them to do so. From such accidents as these, you may judge what such management is worth. A Juryman: Can you give us any information as to how we could alter that state of things? The Coroner : Find it out for yourselves. If ;vow will employ a respectable solicitor,c,he wilTsoon set you in the way. A Juryman: But we are very poor. In the course of some further discussion, Mr. Driffield ob- served that the people of Widnes brought their works to the line, and they must take the consequences. A Juryman said that when the line was first made there were not so many level Crossings as there were new. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." A Juryman said he was not satisfied with the position of the company. Mr. Ferrand : The same thing may happen to-morrow if you choose to take a short-cut. The Coroner said he sympathised with some of the ob- servations made by members of the jury, but he could not help them. If the company had a management at Liver- pool, something might be done in such a case, but not under the present London centralization plan. The public sanc- tioned the plan of London management; nd, in fact, they lived on the company's profits. It was stated that the Local Board had been successful in negotiating with the London and North-Western Company to abolish several of the crossings, and the Coroner said hp was very glad to hear this. A Juryman : We must put better men on the Local Board. The Coroner : Yes, the Local Board members are the right parties. Set them to work. This terminated the enquiry.

FRODSTIAM. , CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS. —OR Sunday nst, two sermons were preached in the Iron Church, Frodsham, by the Rev. W. H. Payne-Smith, M.A , smior student of Christ Church, Oxford, the proceeds being in aia of the funds of the Church Sunday Schools. The collections only amounted to £9 Os. 2d. against £l7 17s. last year, when the Rev. H. Linton, M.A., Canon of Christ Church, Oxford, preached. The falling of in the collection is doubtless due to the want of public notice of the intended special sermons.

div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

MONDAY—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes (chairman) and Mr. S. B. Chadwick. A reuiNTMENT OF OVERsEERS.—A HOLE AND CORNER MEETING ATASTON-BY-SIITrON.—Mr. W. H. Line ker said he wished to make a few remarks to the Bench with reference ' to the nomination of overseers for the township of Aston- by-Sutton. He was instructed by certain ratepayers to ob- ject to the list of names which had been submitted to them, on the following grounds :—The ordinary ratepayers' meet- ing for the nomination of overseers was advertised to be held at noon on the previous Tuesday, but the overseers took r pen themselves to countermand the gathering, and to call a hole-and-corner meeting, which was held at the offices of the assistant overseer, on the evening of the same day. At this meeting the overseers quietly arranged things amongst themselves, as, he believed, there were only three ratepayers present (including the two overseers). On this ground, he asked the Bench to refuse to accept the list of names which had been submitted to them, on the ground that they were not proper men to have the convening of a public meeting in a township like Aston-by-Sutton. Mr. James Robinson, the assistant overse-r, was present, and had the rate book with him. Upon examing it, the Bench I would probably find the names of some gentlemen who were very suitable for the office.—The Chairman asked if the ' meeting referred to, and held at night, was properly con- vened 7—Mr.Linaker. : No, it was an illegal meeting.—Mr. Bankes : It appears to have been truly an Illegal meeting. Does Mr. Robinson object to anything. which Mr. Linaker , has stated 7—Mr. Robinson : What be has stated ie cor- rect. The mreting was illegal.—The Chairman said that seeing the meeting was illegal, he wished to know if Mr. Linaker had any seggestion to make to the Bench as to any gentlemen who were qualified to accept such an appoint- ment.—Mr. Linaker eaid:that, being appealed to on the subject, he begged to suggest that Mr. George Percival, of Park-side Farm, and Mr. Win. Wilkinson, of Aston Heath Farm, should be appointed. He believed they were the largest ratepayers in the township, and he thought they were well qualified to undertake the ieeponsibilities incident to the office.—The Chairman : Mr. George Percival and Mr. Wm. Wilkinson are appointed to the office.—The fol- lowing is e list of the'overseers appointed in the case of other townships :—Astaa Grange : Thomas Lewis arid , Thomas Walton; Clifton : Wm. Baker and Joseph Stokes; I Norton : Thomas Percival and David Bennett ; Halton : Thomas Wright and Hugh Rowe; Runcorn: Win. Hand- ley and Win. Whittaker ; Stockhant : Joseph Walworth Baguley and Daniel Tinsley Baguley ; Sutton: William Fowles and Thomas Rigby ; Weston : Richard Clarke and Thomas Ford. A NEW WAY OF EVADING TDE CANAL BOATS' ACT.--• Joseph Kay was summoned by Mr. Farrington, inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, for using a canal 1, boat called the William as a dwelling for seven people, when it was only registered for three.—The Inspector proved I seeing the boat at Norton, on the 17th ult., and that there were seven people upon it. He spoke to defendant about \ the matter, and he said he could not do otherwise, as he was poor. The Authority had no desire to press the case ; but they wished boat people to know that they could not be per- mitted to evade the Act in the manner they were doing at present, by sending their children forward when starting from a terminus, and taking them en board afterwards. In this way many of them succeeded in evading both the Education and the Canal Boats' Act. He did not consider the present a bad Case.—lletendant was only fined is. and costs 9s. 6d. A RAID ON FOOD ADuLTERATORs.—Thomas Williams was summoned by Superintendent Williamson for unlaw- fully selling 4oz. of mustard which were not of the nature, substance, ard quality of the article demanded by P.C. Bos- sons, and to his prejudice. The officer stated that on the Bth ult. be was instructed by the Superintendent to obtain him a number of samples of the food sold in the town, for the purpose of sending them to Mr. J. Carter Bell, the county analyst. He visited the defendant's shop in Canal- street, and bought 4oz. mustard, for which he paid twopence. He bought the mustard from agirl in the shop, and told her that he should send it to the public analyst, and if she wished to have a quantity of it to keep, she could do. The girl then said she would fetch her mother. —Superintendent Williamson said that on the Bth ult, be received a parcel of mustard from the last withess, and on, the 9th ult. gave it to the Public Analyst, at Weller Broughton, near Manchester. On the 16th ult. he received a certificate from the analyst stating that the mustard was adulterated with 35 per cent. of farinaceous matter. After defendant had been summoned, he came to see witness and stated that he had bought the mustard at a sale, at the shop formerly kept by Mr. Moss, Church-street, and did not I know what it contained. Defendant also said he did not sell 1 half a pound of mustard in ells months. Witness did not I consider the ease a flagrant one. The Bench said defendant would be fined ss. and costs, 16a. 6d., and they hoped it would be a caution to him to keep a better article in future. —John Atkin was charged with baying, on the Bth ult., sold four ounces of mustard to P.C. Bossons, under similar circumstances. The officer proved purchasing the mustard at defendant's shop, and Superintendent Williamson stated that on the 16th ult. he received a certificate from the county analyst to the effect that it contained 25 per cent. of farinaceous matter. Defendant was fined ss. and costs, 183. 64. A POLICEMAN...CATCHES A TARTAR.—Rohert Tneham was summoned for having, on the Bth ult., unlawfully refused to sell to P.C. Bossons a quantity of coffee; and his wife,

The following report has been issued to the members of this Association :—" The committee have much pleasure in submitting their report of the transactions of the Association during the past year. The thanks of the Association are due to the president, who very kindly again engaged Mr. Noble, of London, to deliver one of his popular lectures. The lecture was delivered in the Drill Hall, on the 10th of January, and the subject was 'Free Trade in Land.' A large audience assembled, and the lecturer's lucid exposition of the origin and effect of our land laws was listened to with much interest. At the first meeting of the General Com- mittee, held January 16th, the gentlemen who had held office during the preceding year were re-elected, viz., Mr. E. K. Muspratt, president; Mr. E. Carey, vice-president; Mr. Robert Shaw, treasurer; and Mr. Martin Taylor, hon. secre- tary; these four gentlemen were further appointed to repre- sent the Association on the General Council of the National Reform Union, and, in conjunction with Mr. Timmis, also on the General Council of the National Liberal Federation. The thanks of the Association are also due to Mr. R. H. Davies, who defrayed the expense of the Drill Hall, and arranged for a lecture, on February 11th, by W. S. Caine,l Esq., on ' Our Scientific Frontier,' illustrated with 'large maps;' they very excellent lecture was also very well attended, and much appriciated. In March last, Lord Beaconsfield having at length decided upon making his long- threatened appeal to the country, your organisation was severely tested by the necessity, at very short notice, of assisting in the contest of this division of the county. Our party was thoroughly united, full of zeal, and worked well; theme merit xoe fc ia:ii:-..e CG °I amdisnt iotnt eee, s met brilliantdaily; v i publicetory i meetings Midlothian, ißvaatshabnonine,cEidscjen. hmealdd,eabtyonmero. f J. Lhi.cmh uosuprractatnadtidsesm, and the Hon. Captain Molyneux were present, and spoke to a densely crowded and enthusiastic audience. The announce- eWe t'i nGg., I that will not easily be forgotten by those present. The I Liberal candidates were defeated; your committee has, how- I ever, no reason to be dissatisfied with the work done by the Widnes Liberals. So far as can be ascertained under the ballot, we were successful in polling our full strength, and in giving a substantial majority in our district. On the 23rd May, the Executive Committee met to receive the resignation of the general secretary, Mr. W. Herrington I Jones, as, owing to business engagements outside of Widnes, he could not conveniently continue to fulfil the duties of the I office, and his resignation having been accepted, Mr. H. B. Shores was appointed his successor. The annual picnic took place July 22nd, at Blackpool, where arrangements had been made with the Raikes Hall Gardens Co. for the enter- tainment of the party, consisting of abcut 300 persons; in the evening addresses were delivered by Messrs.E. K. Mus- pratt, J. Hampden Jackson, R. Shaw, E. Carey, M. Taylor, J. L. Muspratt, dm., and the following resolutions were unanimously passed :-Ist. That this meeting desires to ex- press its satisfaction at the result of the late general election and the formation of the present Cabinet with Mr. Glad- stone as Prime Minist.r. 2n4. That this meeting deplores thehbstruction to public business which seems to have been adopted as a policy by a section of the Tory party, in the vain hope of preventing legislation in the interests of the people of Great Britain and Ireland, and this meeting trusts that Parliament will not be prorogued until the bills intro- duced, and more especially the Compensation for Disturbance, the Hares and Rabbits, the Employers' Liability, and the Burial Bills have received the sanction of the Legislature. During the year a number of pamphlets bearing upon various subjects of interest to the party have been distributed by the Association. In conclusion, the committee have to report that the registration work of 1880 has resulted in a nett gain of three votes to the Liberal party in the Widnes polling district. —H. B. SHORES, general secretary."

WIDNES POLICE COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. A. Fletcher (chairman) and Mr. W. Pilkington. VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A COUNTY COURT BAILIFF.—John Mahoney, in custody, was charged with committing a vofiotlhenetsats,sialuelitenos c n Mr. nAtlyeacanoduerrt.—Atmwre.ll,Hotniseboanf dt,hewbhaoiltitlips. peared for the complainant, briefly opened the case, and hsaurcdiliy anneacesssasaurlyt_hec sohniopuladindawnetllsaoind naturela9ttiht was iatos. f ehheantasoreinrei serious hutesh he had to execute a warrant of com- mitment upon a woman named Mrs. Tinsley, living at Mill- brow, Appleton. On going to her house, a large number of people assembled, and the prisoner became very violent in his conduct. He told him that he was an officer of the St. Helens County Court, and only acting in his official capa- city. He also warned him that if be committed any assault, I or interfered with him in the discharge of his duty, he would lay himself open to serious consequences. Prisoner did not take the slightest notice of what he said, but ran at him and gave him a very violent Vow in the mouth, which I cut his lip.and loosened two of his teeth. Mahoney next made a running kick at him, which he managed to parry,' and gave his assailant a telling blow with his stick. I Prisoner then became infuriated, ran into the house, and I came out with the poker. The neighbours seized Mahoney,l and, after imploring him not to assault him with so dan- gerous a weapon, they managed to get him into the house. Mr. Thomas Wheat, chemist, Dickson-street, said he was. the I plaintiff in the County Court action, and he accompanied the bailiff to the house for the purpose of pointing out the woman. He believed that the prisoner had married Mrs. Tinsley's eldest daughter. He corroborated the statement of the complainant as to the assault —On the part of the prisoner it was alleged that the bailiff struck him first-- Prisoner was fined 303. and costs 9s. ed., and had also to pay 10s. 6d. advocate's fee, and 2s. 61 to a witness. STEALING SCRAP IRON AND LEAD FROM A WORKS.— Elizabeth Bushed, Catherine Cannon, and Mary Ann I Hyman, three dirty looking young women, were charged I with stealing scrap iron and lead from the chemical works of Messrs. Mort and Liddell, on the Marsh.—Mr. William Hare, of Moor-lane, manager to the proseeutors, sid that morning, about half-past ten, he saw the prisoners trespass- ing in the works, and picking up scrap iron, a chain, and sonic rope, value 35. 64., which they put into bags. P.C. Ross proved the apprehension of the prisoners. Bushell was sent to prison one month, and the other prisoners were each committed 14 days. The hearing of two or three caseswas adjourned by Mutual consent. There was also one which Mr. Fletcher could not try, owing to the fact that he is interested in the London and North-Western Company. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Uossage. ALLEGED TIIEFF OF £lO AND Two SILVER Warrclufs. James Lee, a middle-aged man, was charged with having, on the 7th May, 1870, stolen from the house of George Pownton, Anne-streer, West, £lO in cash, and two watches, value £l2 IN.—The Inspector of Police stated that on the 30th April, 1879, at about nine o'clock at night, the pri- soner visited the house ef the prosecutor, and claimed to be a relation of Mrs. Pownton. After some conversation, the prosecutor's wife recognised him, and agreed to take him in. Prisoner remained there until the following Wednesday. As , he was a joiner by trade, Mr. Pownton set him to work to I make a pair of drawers. On the 7th of May he commenced I to do this, and in the afternoon went out, alleging that he wanted aguage, and was going to a shop for it. He did not return, and about six o'clock the same evening Mrs. Pown- ton went upstairs, and found that a drawer in the front Loom I had been broken open, £lO taken from the cash-book, and two watches stolen. She gave information to the police, and on Thursday the prisoner was apprehended as he was coming out of Northampton Gaol, where he had been suffering im- prisonment for larceny.—Mrs. Pownton gave corroborative evidence, and the prisoner was remanded until Monday.

it. The Coroner: You should do it again. Mr. Ferrand : I suppose we shall have to do it again. By the Coroner: The witness, in cross-examination, said he let the two•men thro'ugh the gates and locked them.— Did not you let these men through the gates sooner than you ought to have done? No, sir.—Should not you have I had these gates locked a little sooner? No, sir.—What is the use of giving you the locks if you do not lock the men out? I begin to understand, now, that your railway com- pany sometimes declines to put locks on such places when they are asked to do so. A jury asked the company to pat a couple of locks on gates the other day, but they declined. Mr. Ferrand : If you put locks all over, you would not prevent men getting on the line. I should think that the members of the jury must know this to be the case. In reply to a juryman, ths witness said there were locks on the gates belonging, to the wickets. The Coroner: Yes, but the locks were put on to prevent these men from going through. By the Police Inspector : Just before the accident he knew that the passenger train was due, but it was near Widnes then. The gentlemen on the jury were well aware that if he locked the wickets when the train was at Widnes, he got all sorts of insults from the people. They had no rules about lacking the gates before a train was due. By a Juryman: He had not time to set his signals against the passenger train when the two men stepped into the four foot. By the Inspector: lie certainly did say something par- ticular to the men when he saw them in the four foot—he told them to get out of the way, and stand by the wall. They did not seem to take any notice of him. Burgess appeared , sober, tottt he considered Fawcett to be rather the worse for drink.

TATE OPERATIVE COTTON SPINNERs' Assoctamosrop LaNcasume.—The annual report for 1880 of the Amalga- mated Association of Operative Cotton Spinners, dco., of Lancashire and adjoining counties has been issued. The members are congratulated on the improved aspect of affairs as compared with the previous year. From some iemarks made by the general secretary we infer that the members of the Association have net yet arrived at the point where it is considered advisable to give their accumulated balances, but this course appearing to have given rise to some misconcep- tion, he suggests that in future it should be done. The in come for the year is reported to be £22,096 18s. 74.; thel ditar” , Ll 6 452 18s. id., leaving a balance of £5,644 expert 50., which is stated to more than counterbdance the loss on the previous year's operations. That spinners are much more generally employed than during 1879 is shown by the amount expended in out-of-work benefit (£4.220 6,. 111 d.) being less than half the amount paid in 1879. , Disputes have cost £2554 Os. 94.; the amount for the previous year being £7,747 lie. 7a. Breakdowns and stop- pages absorb £2,895 14s. 11d.; accident, £BO4 13s. 3d.;. while emigration, leaving trade, superannuation and other benefits, take the remainder of the amount named. In some remarks on the Factory Acts approval is expressed of the I activity which has of late characterised the inspectors. Open overtime working is said to be almost stamped out, and spasmodic attempts to re-introduce the system have in- variably failed. A Parliamentary return is given firm which it appears that only a very small proportion of the inspectors appointed since 1867 have ever been examined. On this topic the general secretary says So far as recards the subjects in which candidates for inspectors are examined appiicanes passed i t intelligence, i sdbou doubtless it is simply useless for the special object in view.
